129075.q: What does a farmer do on the farm?
a: Looks after animals and grows plants
Drives a train across the country
129075.e: Farmers look after cows, pigs or chickens and grow grain, potatoes or vegetables.
129075.m: A lot of our food comes from farms.

129076.q: Which vehicle does a farmer often need in the field?
129076.e: With the tractor the farmer pulls trailers, a plough or a mower. This makes work in the fields much easier.
129076.m: The tractor is the favourite vehicle on the farm.

129077.q: Which material does a joiner work with most?
129077.e: Joiners make furniture such as tables, cupboards or beds out of wood. They also make doors and kitchens.
129077.m: The joiner turns wood into furniture.

129078.q: Who needs a plane to make wood smooth?
129078.e: With the plane, the joiner takes thin shavings off the wood. This makes the wood nice and smooth and straight.

129079.q: Which tools does a hairdresser need every day?
a: A brush and a paint roller
129079.e: The hairdresser cuts hair with scissors and a comb. She often needs a hairdryer too.
129079.m: Scissors and a comb belong in a hair salon.

129080.e: A hair salon has mirrors, chairs and washbasins. That is where hairdressers wash, cut and style hair.
129080.m: The hairdresser works in a salon.

129081.q: What does a train driver do?
129081.e: The train driver sits at the front in the driver's cab and brings the train safely and on time to its destination.
129081.m: The train driver drives the train.

129082.q: Where does the train driver sit during the journey?
a: Right at the front in the driver's cab
On the roof of the train
In the last carriage with the suitcases
129082.e: The driver's cab is at the front of the train. From there the driver can see the tracks and the signals.
129082.m: The train driver sits at the front of the train.

129083.q: What does a nurse do in hospital?
129083.e: Nurses take temperatures, give medicines and help patients in everyday life.
129083.m: Nurses help sick people get well.

129085.q: Where does a polymechanic usually work?
129085.e: In the workshop there are big machines for working metal. That is where the polymechanic works.

129086.q: What does a cook do in a restaurant?
129086.e: The cook chops, fries and cooks in the restaurant kitchen. Then the food is served to the guests.
129086.m: The cook cooks for lots of guests.

129087.q: Why do cooks often wear a white hat?
a: So that no hair falls into the food
So that they don't get cold
So that you can see them from far away
So that the sun doesn't dazzle them
129087.e: The tall white chef's hat keeps the hair together. That way no hair falls into the food.
129087.m: The chef's hat protects food from hair.

129089.q: Why should only experts work on cables and sockets?
a: Electricity can give you a serious shock
129089.e: An electric shock can seriously injure people. That is why only trained electricians work on cables and sockets.

129091.q: Which tool does a gardener use to give plants water?
129091.e: Plants get water from the watering can or the hose. Without water they would wilt.
129091.m: Plants need water from the watering can.

129092.q: Who helps when your dog is ill?
129092.e: The vet examines and treats sick animals. She also vaccinates dogs and cats.
129092.m: Sick animals go to the vet.

129093.q: Mia is taking her cat to be vaccinated. Where does she go?
129093.e: At the vet's surgery, animals are examined, vaccinated and treated.

129094.q: What is one of the jobs of police officers?
a: They keep people safe and maintain order
They bake bread for the village
They plant trees in the forest
129094.e: The police help at accidents, direct traffic and make sure everyone sticks to the rules.

129095.q: What does the fire brigade do besides putting out fires?
a: It also helps with accidents and floods
129095.e: The fire brigade rescues people and animals and helps with accidents, floods and storm damage.
129095.m: The fire brigade helps in many emergencies.

129096.e: Pilots fly planes or helicopters and bring passengers safely to their destination.
129096.m: The pilot flies high in the sky.

129097.q: What is the place where the pilot sits in the plane called?
129097.e: The cockpit is right at the front of the plane. It has lots of buttons, screens and the controls.
129097.m: The plane is flown from the cockpit.

129098.e: Postmen and postwomen deliver the post to people's letterboxes.

129099.q: What do people in German-speaking Switzerland often call the postman?
129099.e: In Switzerland many people say “Pöstler” or “Pöstlerin” for the person who brings letters and parcels. “Lokführer” is a train driver, “Bauarbeiter” a builder and “Kassierer” a cashier.
129099.m: “Pöstler” is the Swiss word for a postman.

129100.q: What does a teacher do at school?
129100.e: Teachers explain reading, writing, maths and much more. They help children learn.

129101.q: What does the teacher often write on in the classroom?
129101.e: On the board or a big screen, the teacher shows what the class is learning.
129101.m: The board is the class's big exercise book.

129102.q: What does an IT specialist mainly work with?
129102.e: IT specialists write programs, set up computers and help when something doesn't work.
129102.m: The IT specialist speaks the language of computers.

129103.q: Who writes the programs for games and apps?
129103.e: Every game and every app is a program. IT specialists write the commands for the computer.
129103.m: Behind every app there is a program.

a: Walls out of bricks and concrete
129104.e: On the building site, bricklayers build walls out of bricks and concrete.
129104.m: The bricklayer builds brick by brick.

129105.q: Which tool does a bricklayer need for the mortar?
129105.e: With the trowel, the bricklayer spreads mortar between the bricks. That way they hold together firmly.

129106.q: Where does a bricklayer usually work?
129106.e: New houses go up on building sites. Bricklayers work there together with many other tradespeople.
129106.m: On the building site, a house grows.

129107.q: Why do people on a building site wear a helmet?
129107.e: Things can fall down on a building site. The helmet protects the head from injuries.

129108.q: Why does a baker often get up very early?
a: So that the bread is fresh in the morning
Because the bakery is closed in the evening
Because dough only rises at night
129108.e: Many people want fresh bread for breakfast. That is why bakers often start in the middle of the night or early in the morning.
129108.m: Getting up early brings fresh bread.

129109.q: Where is the bread baked in a bakery?
129109.e: In the hot oven, dough turns into crusty bread.
129109.m: The oven makes the bread crusty.

129111.q: Where do you pay for your shopping in a shop?
129111.e: At the till the goods are scanned, and you pay with cash or a card.

129112.q: What does a carpenter build out of wood?
129112.e: Carpenters build large wooden structures, for example the frame of a roof or whole wooden houses.
129112.m: The carpenter builds the roof out of wood.

129113.q: What is the difference between a joiner and a carpenter?
a: The carpenter builds large wooden structures, the joiner makes furniture
The joiner only works with metal
There is no difference at all
129113.e: Both work with wood. The carpenter builds roofs and wooden houses, the joiner makes furniture, doors and kitchens.

129114.q: Who do you call when water is dripping from the pipe?
129114.e: Plumbers lay water pipes and fit washbasins, toilets and showers.
129114.m: If it drips, the plumber helps.

129115.q: Who needs a pipe wrench for work?
129115.e: With the pipe wrench, the plumber tightens or loosens pipes and nuts.

129116.q: What does a painter do on a building site?
129116.e: Painters paint walls, outside walls, windows and doors. This makes a house look nice and protects it.
129116.m: The painter brings colour into the house.

129117.q: Which tool does a painter need for big walls?
129117.e: With a paint roller, the painter can paint large areas quickly and evenly.

129118.q: What does a mechanic do in the garage?
129118.e: In the garage the mechanic changes tyres and oil, for example, and repairs whatever is broken on the car.
129118.m: In the garage, the car gets fit again.

129119.q: Which tool does a mechanic often need?
129119.e: With a spanner, the mechanic tightens or loosens screws and nuts.

129120.e: Foresters look after the forest. They decide which trees are cut down and where new ones are planted.
129120.m: The forester looks after the forest.

129121.q: Who cuts down trees in the forest with a chainsaw?
129121.e: Forestry workers work in the forest. They cut down trees, plant young trees and look after forest paths.
129121.m: Foresters and forestry workers work in the forest.

129122.e: At the dentist your teeth are checked. If a tooth has a hole, the dentist fixes it with a filling.
129122.m: The dentist keeps your teeth healthy.

129123.q: Why do schoolchildren go for regular dental check-ups?
a: So that holes are found early
So that you never have to brush again
129123.e: At a check-up, small holes are spotted early. Then fixing them is easier and hurts less.

a: Hands out medicines and gives advice on them
129124.e: You get medicines at the chemist. The pharmacist explains how to take them properly.
129124.m: At the chemist you get advice and medicine.

129125.q: What does a bus driver do?
129125.e: Bus drivers follow a timetable from stop to stop and take people where they want to go.
129125.m: The bus driver takes you to the stop.

129126.q: How does the bus driver know when to be where?
129126.e: The timetable shows when the bus leaves from each stop. The driver sticks to it.
129126.m: The timetable tells you when the bus comes.

a: A place where small children are looked after
129128.e: Kita is short for Kindertagesstätte, a day nursery. Children are looked after there while their parents work.
129128.m: A Kita is a day nursery.

129129.e: Butchers, today called meat specialists, prepare meat and also make sausages from it.

129130.q: What does a dressmaker, officially a clothing designer, do?
129130.e: Clothing designers sew clothes and alter them, for example when a pair of trousers is too long.
129130.m: Clothes are made with a needle and thread.

129131.q: Who needs a sewing machine for work?
129131.e: With a sewing machine you can sew fabric much faster than by hand.

129132.q: Leo has a flat tyre on his bike. Who can help him?
129132.e: Bike mechanics, officially bicycle mechanics, fix tyres, brakes and chains.

129133.e: Florists work in a flower shop. They make bouquets and flower decorations for celebrations.
129133.m: The florist works magic with flowers.

129134.q: Who steers a ship on the lake?
129134.e: Passenger boats run on Swiss lakes. At the front, the captain steers the boat.
129134.m: On a ship, the captain is at the wheel.

129135.q: What does a zookeeper do at the zoo?
a: Feeds the animals and cleans the enclosures
Sells ice cream at the entrance
129135.e: Zookeepers make sure the zoo animals are well. They feed, clean and watch the animals.
129135.m: At the zoo, the zookeeper looks after the animals.

129136.q: Who comes in the ambulance when someone is injured?
129136.e: Paramedics give first aid and take injured people to hospital. Their number is 144.

129137.q: What is an apprenticeship, explained simply?
a: A way of learning a job after school
129137.e: In an apprenticeship you learn a job directly at a company and go to vocational school as well. Many young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship.
129137.m: In an apprenticeship you learn a job.

129138.q: What do you call someone who is doing an apprenticeship?
129138.e: Someone doing an apprenticeship is called an apprentice. In Switzerland the official word today is “learner”.
129138.m: Someone doing an apprenticeship is an apprentice.

129139.q: Where does an apprentice learn most of their job?
129139.e: The training company is the firm where you do your apprenticeship. There a trainer shows you how the work is done.
129139.m: You learn the work at the training company.

129140.q: Where do apprentices go besides working at the company?
129140.e: At vocational school, apprentices learn the knowledge they need for their job, as well as general subjects.
129140.m: Work at the company, knowledge at vocational school.

129141.q: Do apprentices in Switzerland get paid for their work?
a: No, they have to pay themselves
129141.e: Apprentices work at the company and get an apprentice's wage every month. It goes up a little with each year of the apprenticeship.
129141.m: Apprentices already earn their own money.

129142.q: Nina wants to find out whether she would like being a cook. What can she do later on?
a: Try it out for a few days in a kitchen
Forget about the job straight away
129142.e: On a taster placement you work at a company for a few days. That way you see what the job is really like.
129142.m: A taster placement means trying out a job.

129143.q: When do young people in Switzerland usually do a taster placement?
a: At lower secondary school, aged about 13 to 15
129143.e: Choosing a career usually begins at lower secondary school. Then young people try out different jobs.
129143.m: Taster placements happen at lower secondary school.

129144.q: Lara is very good at drawing and making things. Which job would suit her well?
129144.e: Graphic designers design posters, books and logos. If you like drawing, you have a good strength for it.
129144.m: Your strengths show you jobs that suit you.

129145.q: Tim likes building things out of wood in his free time. Which job might he like?
129145.e: If you like building with wood, you might find a great job as a joiner or carpenter.
129145.m: A hobby can become a job.

129146.q: At home, Sara likes helping with the cooking best. Which job suits her?
129146.e: If you like cooking and trying out new recipes, you can become a cook.
129146.m: If you like cooking, you can become a cook.

129147.q: Jonas likes helping other people and is patient. Which job suits him?
129147.e: Nursing needs patience and enjoying helping others. Nurses look after sick and elderly people.
129147.m: Helping is fun, at work too.

129148.q: Elin likes taking old devices apart. Which job suits her?
129148.e: If you are curious about how machines work, you will enjoy technical jobs such as polymechanic or electronics technician.
129148.m: Curiosity about technology suits technical jobs.

129149.q: Ben likes being outside, even in the rain. Which job suits him?
129149.e: Forestry workers almost always work outside in the forest, in all weathers.
129149.m: If you like being outdoors, there are outdoor jobs.

129150.q: What does a forestry worker wear for protection when working with a chainsaw?
a: A helmet, ear protection and cut-resistant trousers
A sun hat, a T-shirt and sandals
A woolly hat, tracksuit bottoms and trainers
129150.e: The chainsaw is loud and dangerous. A helmet, ear protection and special trousers protect the forestry worker.
129150.m: Protective clothing protects you during dangerous work.

129151.q: Who moves heavy loads through the air on a building site?
129151.e: Crane operators sit high up in the cab and lift heavy parts such as concrete slabs into place.
129151.m: The crane lifts the heavy things.

129152.q: Who puts the tiles on the roof?
129152.e: Roofers cover the roof with tiles. That way the house stays dry.
129152.m: The roofer makes the roof watertight.

129153.q: Where do you get new glasses?
129153.e: Opticians test your eyes and make glasses that suit you.
129153.m: The optician helps you see better.

129154.q: Which job is particularly well known and famous in Switzerland?
129154.e: Switzerland is known all over the world for its watches. Watchmakers build and repair them with fine tools.

129155.q: Why does a watchmaker need a magnifying glass?
a: Because the parts in a watch are very small
Because otherwise she can't hear anything
129155.e: A watch has tiny wheels and screws. With the magnifying glass the watchmaker sees them big.
129155.m: A magnifying glass makes small things big.

129156.q: What does a chimney sweep do?
a: Bakes pizza in a wood-fired oven
129156.e: Chimney sweeps clean chimneys and check heating systems so that no fires start.
129156.m: The chimney sweep keeps the chimney clean.

129157.q: What colour is a chimney sweep's work clothing traditionally?
129157.e: Chimney sweeps traditionally wear black clothes. Soot from the chimney shows less on them.

129158.q: What does a baker need to make dough?
129158.e: For bread you mainly need flour, water, salt and yeast. The yeast makes the dough rise.
129158.m: Flour, water, salt and yeast: that's how bread is made.

129159.q: Who makes fine gateaux, cakes and chocolates?
129159.e: Pastry chefs are experts in sweet things. They make gateaux, cakes and chocolates.
129159.m: Sweet things come from the pastry chef.

129160.q: Which jobs work together when a new house is built?
129160.e: A house needs many jobs: bricklayers build the walls, carpenters the roof, electricians the electrics and painters the colour.

129161.q: Why do some nurses also work at night?
a: Because sick people need help at night too
Because the hospital is tidied up at night
Because they want to sleep during the day
Because more visitors come at night
129161.e: In a hospital there must always be people there, at night and at weekends too. That is why there are shifts.
129161.m: In hospital, help is there round the clock.

129162.q: Which statement about jobs is true?
a: Girls and boys can learn any job
Only adults over 40 can learn a job
129162.e: Every job is open to everyone. There are female pilots, female joiners, male nurses and male nursery teachers.
129162.m: Every job is there for everyone.

129163.q: Who builds and repairs the roads?
129163.e: Road builders lay new roads, surface them with tarmac and fill holes.
129163.m: The road builder makes the way smooth.

129164.q: Who drives the goods by road from the warehouse to the shops?
129164.e: Lorry drivers, officially road transport specialists, drive goods from warehouses to shops.
129164.m: The lorry brings the goods to the shop.

129165.q: Who makes sure everything in the school building is clean and in good repair?
129165.e: Caretakers look after the school building, repair small things and keep everything in order.
129165.m: The caretaker looks after the school building.

129166.e: In the library you can borrow books. The librarian sorts the books and helps you find them.
129166.m: Librarians help you in the library.

129167.q: Dad pays in a restaurant and says to the waitress: “Keep the change.” What does he mean?
a: She may keep the change as a tip
The food was seasoned just right
He wants the change in coins
The bill should be counted again
129167.e: With “Keep the change” you say that the staff may keep the rest of the money. This little thank-you is called a tip.
129167.m: “Keep the change” means the rest is a thank-you.

129168.q: Lea gets a voucher from a bookshop for her birthday. What can she do with it?
a: Pay with it in the bookshop like money
Change it for cash at a cash machine
Shop in any shop in the world
Use it as a bus ticket
129168.e: A voucher is a piece of paper or a card with a value. You can pay with it in the shop named on it, but usually not anywhere else.
129168.m: A voucher is money for one particular shop.

129169.q: The game Noah wants to buy says “sold out” in the shop. What does that mean?
a: You may only look at the game
129169.e: “Sold out” means all of them have already been sold. Noah has to wait until the shop gets new ones, or look somewhere else.

129170.q: When in the year is World Savings Day, when many banks invite children to save?
129170.e: World Savings Day is at the end of October. Many banks invite children to empty their money boxes and bring the money to their account.
129170.m: World Savings Day is at the end of October.

129171.q: What can you keep in a safe deposit box at the bank?
129171.e: A safe deposit box is a small lockable box in a secure room at the bank. People put valuables in it that are not safe enough at home.
129171.m: Valuables go in the safe deposit box.

129172.q: How is a lot of cash taken safely to a bank?
a: In an ordinary letter by post
In the boot of a taxi
129172.e: For large amounts of cash there are special vehicles with thick walls and well-trained drivers. That way the money is well protected on the way.
129172.m: Lots of cash travels in an armoured van.

a: A paper roll with the same number of identical coins
A machine that makes new coins
129173.e: A coin roll always holds the same number of coins of the same kind. That way you can count lots of small change quickly and carry it neatly.
129173.m: A coin roll keeps coins neatly together.

129174.q: In the past, children at the bank often got a savings book. What was written in it?
a: How much money is in the savings account
The names of all the bank staff
129174.e: The bank wrote every deposit and withdrawal in the savings book. That way you could always see how much you had saved. Today you often see this in an app.
129174.m: The savings book showed how much had been saved.

129175.q: The Keller family is going on holiday to Italy. Where can they change francs into euros?
a: At a bank or bureau de change
129175.e: In Italy people pay with euros. Banks and bureaux de change exchange francs for euros.
129175.m: You can change money at the bank.

129176.q: Why do you sometimes have to sign something at the bank?
a: So the bank knows how old you are
So you don't forget your name
129176.e: With a signature you write your name in a special way. It confirms that you want something and agree to it.

129177.q: What does the bank use to count lots of banknotes quickly?
129177.e: A money-counting machine runs the notes through at lightning speed and counts them. It often even notices when a note is fake.
129177.m: The machine counts notes faster than any hand.

129178.q: What does a power of attorney for a bank account mean?
a: Another person may also use the account
The account then belongs to the other person
The bank may close the account
129178.e: With a power of attorney, the account holder allows another person to make payments, for example. But the money still belongs to the holder.
129178.m: Power of attorney means: someone else may act for me.

129179.q: What is special about a cooperative bank?
a: It always belongs to the federal government
It has no accounts of its own
129179.e: At a cooperative bank you can buy shares and become a member of the cooperative. The members can then have a say.
129179.m: In a cooperative, the bank belongs to its members.

129180.q: What is the BIC, also called the SWIFT code, used for in a payment abroad?
a: It is the password for online banking
129180.e: The BIC is an international code for a bank. For payments abroad, it helps send the money to the right bank.
129180.m: The IBAN names the account, the BIC the bank.

129181.q: What is a foreign currency account?
a: An account in euros instead of francs, for example
An account only foreigners may open
An account without an account number
129181.e: A foreign currency account holds money in another currency, such as euros or dollars. That is handy if you often pay or receive money in that currency.
129181.m: Foreign currency account: foreign money, your own account.

a: An account that belongs to several people
An account of the whole municipality
An account run by the school
129182.e: A joint account is in the name of two or more people, for example a couple or flatmates. All holders can use it, depending on what has been agreed.

129183.q: Where can you turn free of charge in Switzerland if you have a dispute with your bank?
a: The SIX stock exchange in Zurich
129183.e: The Swiss Banking Ombudsman is a neutral mediation service. It helps customers free of charge to settle a dispute with a bank without going to court.
129183.m: Dispute with your bank? Go to the ombudsman first.

a: A loan for which securities serve as collateral
A loan only for trips to Italy
A loan secured by your house
129184.e: With a Lombard loan you pledge securities such as shares or bonds. If their value falls sharply, the bank can ask for extra security.

129185.q: What is stored at the ZEK, the Swiss Central Office for Credit Information?
a: Details of loans, leasing and card agreements
The balances of all savings accounts
129185.e: The ZEK collects details of loans, leasing agreements and card accounts, and also of payment defaults. Banks check there before giving a new loan.
129185.m: If you do not pay, you leave traces at the ZEK.

129186.q: What usually happens to the account of a person who has died?
a: It is blocked until the heirs are proven
The money goes straight to the bank
Anyone with the card may withdraw money
129186.e: When the bank learns of the death, it usually blocks the account. Only with proof, for example a certificate of inheritance, can the heirs use it.
129186.m: After a death, the certificate of inheritance decides, not the card.

a: A note from the doctor saying you were ill
129187.e: In a doctor's certificate, the doctor confirms that someone was ill and could not go to school or work. Adults often need it for their employer.
129187.m: A doctor's certificate shows: I really was ill.

129188.q: Your friend is ill in bed. What do you wish her?
129188.e: With “Get well soon”, you wish someone who is ill that they will soon be healthy again. A card or a phone call can cheer them up.
129188.m: Someone who is ill is pleased to hear “Get well soon”.

a: She helps you move well again with exercises
She sells medicines in the pharmacy
She cleans teeth at the surgery
129189.e: After an injury or when you are in pain, the physiotherapist shows you exercises. They make muscles and joints strong and flexible again.
129189.m: Physio means practising until it works again.

129190.q: Mia has a cough. Her brother still has tablets from the doctor. May she just take them?
a: No, they are only meant for her brother
Yes, a cough is always the same
Yes, if she only takes two
129190.e: The doctor chooses a medicine and the amount specially for one person. For another child it can be wrong or even dangerous.

a: A village fair with rides and stalls
A song you sing in the evening
A cow with a big bell
129191.e: A Chilbi is a cheerful fair in a village or town. There are roundabouts, bumper cars, stalls with sweets and candyfloss.
129191.m: At the Chilbi everything goes round and round.

129192.q: Which sweet, brown treat in small pieces do people often buy at markets in Switzerland?
129192.e: Magenbrot is small pieces of gingerbread dough with a shiny, sweet glaze. People like to buy it in a little bag at markets and at the Chilbi.

129193.q: What is the gingerbread with an almond filling from the Appenzell region called?
129193.e: The Appenzeller Biber is a gingerbread filled with almond paste. A picture, for example a bear, is often pressed onto it.
129193.m: Although “Biber” is German for beaver, here it is gingerbread, not an animal.

129194.q: What colour are the post boxes of Swiss Post?
129194.e: Swiss Post's letter boxes are yellow, just like the PostBuses. That makes them easy to spot everywhere.
129194.m: The post in Switzerland is yellow.

129195.q: Which German municipality is completely surrounded by Swiss territory?
129195.e: Büsingen belongs to Germany but lies in the middle of the canton of Schaffhausen. Such an area is called an exclave. People there often pay in francs.
129195.m: Büsingen: German, but surrounded by Switzerland.

129196.q: How do most voters in Switzerland cast their vote?
a: By raising their hand in the village square
By sending a text to the Federal Council
129196.e: The great majority vote by post. You fill in the ballot paper at home and send it to the municipality in good time with your voting card.

129197.q: Which canton does the number plate code “AI” stand for?
129197.e: Every canton has a two-letter code. AI stands for Appenzell Innerrhoden, AR for Appenzell Ausserrhoden, AG for Aargau and UR for Uri.
129197.m: AI is Innerrhoden, AR is Ausserrhoden.

129198.q: In which two cantons is Italian an official language?
129198.e: In Ticino, Italian is the only official language. In the Grisons it is one of three official languages, for example in the southern valleys such as the Misox and the Puschlav.
129198.m: Italian: Ticino and part of the Grisons.

129199.q: From which place does the cable car up the Säntis leave?
129199.e: The valley station of the Säntis cable car is on the Schwägalp in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. From there the cabin glides up to the highest mountain of the Alpstein.
129199.m: You go up the Säntis from the Schwägalp.

129200.q: What happens at the “Chesslete” in Solothurn?
a: Carnival begins early in the morning with lots of noise
People celebrate the grape harvest by the lake
Decorated cows go up to the alpine pasture
129200.e: The Chesslete opens the Solothurn carnival early in the morning on the Thursday before Lent. Many people wear white nightshirts and make noise to drive away the winter.
129200.m: Chesslete: noise in the morning, carnival begins.

129201.q: What is the Knabenschiessen in Zurich?
a: A shooting competition for young people in September
A football tournament only for boys
A fireworks display on New Year's Eve
A rowing race on Lake Zurich
129201.e: At the Knabenschiessen, young people compete in shooting, today both girls and boys. There is also a big fair at the Albisgüetli.
129201.m: In September young people in Zurich shoot to become the shooting king.

129202.q: What is the last, deciding bout at a Schwingen festival called?
129202.e: In the Schlussgang the best wrestlers face each other. Whoever wins it has a good chance of winning the festival or even the title of king.

129203.q: Which of these things is a wish and not something you need to live?
129203.e: You really need food, a bed and warm clothes. A games console is nice, but you can live perfectly well without one.
129203.m: First come the things you need, then the wishes.

129204.q: The same chocolate costs 2 francs in one shop and 3 francs in another. Where is it cheaper?
129204.e: 2 francs is less than 3 francs. If you compare prices, you save money.

129205.q: Why do people write a shopping list before going shopping?
a: So they only buy what they need
129205.e: With a list you forget nothing and buy fewer things you did not really want.
129205.m: A shopping list protects you from buying things you do not need.

129206.q: You pay for a 7-franc exercise book with a 10-franc note. How much do you get back?
129206.e: 10 francs minus 7 francs makes 3 francs change.
129206.m: Change is what you paid minus the price.

129207.q: Elia pays for 12 francs’ worth of colouring pencils with a 20-franc note. How much change does he get?
129207.e: 20 minus 12 makes 8. Elia gets 8 francs back.
129207.m: Always do a quick sum to check your change.

129208.q: How many 5-centime coins do you need to make 1 franc?
129208.e: 1 franc has 100 centimes. 100 divided by 5 makes 20 coins.

129209.q: How many 2-franc coins add up to 10 francs?

129210.q: How many 50-franc notes are worth the same as one 100-franc note?

129211.q: How many 100-franc notes are worth the same as one 1000-franc note?

129212.q: Lina wants a book for 12 francs. She already has 8 francs. How much more does she need?
129212.e: 12 minus 8 makes 4. Lina still has to save 4 francs.
129212.m: What is missing is the price minus your savings.

129213.q: Every week Jan puts 2 francs in his money box. How much does he have after 10 weeks?
129213.m: Small amounts grow big over time.

129214.q: What is a smart way to handle your pocket money?
a: Spend it all on the first day
129214.e: If you save some, you can afford something bigger later on.
129214.m: Part of your pocket money goes into the money box.

129215.q: Why do adverts show toys looking especially nice and fun?
a: So that you want to buy them
So that you never buy them
Because the bank wants it that way
129215.e: Adverts are meant to make you want to buy something. In real life it is often less exciting.

129216.q: You lend your friend 5 francs. What is important?
a: Agree when he will pay it back
129216.e: If you agree when the money will come back, there are fewer arguments.

129217.q: Jonas borrows 5 francs from his sister for an ice cream. What does he have to do?
a: Buy her an ice cream and keep the money
129217.e: Borrowed money still belongs to his sister. Jonas has to give it back.
129217.m: What you borrow, you give back.

129218.q: Which is cheaper: an apple for 1 franc 50 or an apple for 2 francs?
129218.e: 1 franc 50 is 50 centimes less than 2 francs.

129219.q: A message says: “You have won a mobile phone! Send us your address.” What do you do?
a: Not reply and show it to your parents
Forward it to all your friends
129219.e: Messages like this are often a trick by scammers. Adults help you check them.
129219.m: With prize messages, ask your parents first.

129220.q: How many 1-franc coins do you need to make 5 francs?

129221.q: Why is it good to always have a little money for unexpected things?
a: So you can pay if something breaks
So you never have to work again
129221.e: Sometimes something breaks or you suddenly need money. Then a small reserve helps.
129221.m: A small reserve helps in an emergency.

129222.q: What does it mean to donate money?
a: To give money to help others
To lend money and ask for it back
To save money in an account
To spend money in a shop
129222.e: When you donate, you give money, for example for people in need or for animals.

129223.q: What can you do at a flea market?
129223.e: At a flea market people sell things they no longer need. That way you get a bit of money.
129223.m: What you no longer need, you can sell.

129224.q: Why can it be worth buying a second-hand bike?
a: It then belongs to the bank
129224.e: Second-hand things often cost much less than new ones and still work well.

129225.q: Your bike has a flat tyre. What saves the most money?
129225.e: Repairing an inner tube costs little. A new bike costs much more.
129225.m: Repairing is often cheaper than buying new.

129226.q: You have three 2-franc coins and one 1-franc coin. How much money is that?
129226.e: 3 times 2 francs is 6 francs, plus 1 franc makes 7 francs.
129226.m: First count the same coins, then add them up.

129227.q: A ball costs 10 francs. Today it is half price. How much does it cost?
129227.m: Half price means dividing by two.

129228.q: Lea has 15 francs. She buys a book for 9 francs and a pen for 4 francs. How much does she have left?
129228.e: 9 plus 4 makes 13 francs. 15 minus 13 makes 2 francs.
129228.m: First add everything up, then subtract.

129229.q: Leo has 10 francs. The cinema costs 8 francs and the popcorn 4 francs. What is true?
129229.e: 8 plus 4 makes 12 francs. Leo only has 10 francs, so he is 2 francs short.
129229.m: Before buying, check that you have enough money.

a: A piece of paper saying how much you have to pay
A sum to work out at school
A note saying you have won
129230.e: If you have received something and still have to pay for it, you get a bill. It shows the amount.
129230.m: A bill tells you what you owe.

129231.q: Why is money more practical than swapping things?
a: You can buy almost anything with it
129231.e: With money you do not have to find someone who wants exactly what you have. You simply pay with money.

129232.q: Why do you quickly count your change at the till?
a: So you notice if something is missing
129232.e: Mistakes happen at the till too. If you count, you notice straight away and can ask.

a: A piece of paper or a code you can use to shop in a store
A bill you have to pay
129233.e: A voucher has a certain value. You can use it like money in the right shop.
129233.m: A voucher is like money for a particular shop.

129234.q: You want to buy something online. What do you do?
a: Do it together with your parents
Take your parents’ card on your own
Send money to strangers in a chat
129234.e: There are fake shops on the internet too. Your parents help you shop safely.
129234.m: Only buy online with your parents.

129235.q: Which word is written in big letters on the 1-franc coin?
129235.e: Helvetia is the Latin name for Switzerland. It is on the coin next to the standing figure of Helvetia.
129235.m: Helvetia is the old name for Switzerland.

129236.q: Which is worth more: a 5-franc coin or three 2-franc coins?
129236.e: Three 2-franc coins are 6 francs. The 5-franc coin is worth 5 francs.
129236.m: It is not the number of coins that counts, but their value.

129237.q: You have a 20-centime coin and a 50-centime coin. How much is that altogether?
129237.m: You count centimes like normal numbers.

129238.q: Mia buys 2 croissants at 1 franc 50 each. How much does she pay?
129238.e: 1 franc 50 and another 1 franc 50 makes 3 francs.

129239.q: Ava gets 30 francs. She wants to save half. How much does she save?
129239.e: Half of 30 is 15. Ava saves 15 francs.
129239.m: Saving half is a good rule.

129240.q: Every week Nils spends all his pocket money on collector stickers. What would be smarter?
a: Only use part of it for them
129240.e: If you always spend everything, you can never save for something bigger. Part of it is enough for the stickers.

129241.q: A stranger rings the doorbell and wants money for a collection. You are home alone. What do you do?
a: Give no money and do not open the door
Give him your parents’ bank card
129241.e: When you are alone, you do not give strangers money. Tell your parents about it later.
129241.m: Home alone means no money for strangers.

129242.q: What is the person at the bank called who explains which account suits you?
129242.e: At the bank, customer advisers help people with questions about money.
129242.m: The customer adviser helps with bank questions.

a: An office of a bank in a particular place
A money box shaped like a house
A party held by the bank
129243.e: Big banks have many branches in different places. You can go there and ask questions.
129243.m: A branch is one location of a bank.

129244.q: You have a lot of cash with you on the bus. What is smart?
a: Not showing the money to everyone
Holding the money in your hand and waving
Putting your purse open on the seat
129244.e: Showing a lot of money attracts thieves. So the money stays hidden in your bag.

129245.q: Why is a see-through money box practical for children?
a: You can see the money growing
You do not need a slot
129245.e: When you can see the money growing, saving is more fun.

129246.e: A bike is big and has lots of parts. It costs much more than an ice cream or a pencil.

129247.q: A banknote is torn just a little bit. What is true?
a: You have to throw it away
You may only use it abroad
129247.e: A slightly damaged note keeps its value. If the damage is big, the bank can help.
129247.m: A slightly torn note is still valid.

129248.q: The Huber family wants to go on holiday in the summer. What helps them have enough money?
a: Saving a little every month beforehand
Only thinking about money on holiday
129248.e: If you put something aside early, you have enough money for the holiday in the end.
129248.m: Saving early makes a holiday possible.

129249.q: Which money comes in to you?
a: The money for a new game
The money for an ice cream
The money for a bus ticket
129249.e: A present brings you money. For a game, an ice cream and a ticket you spend money.
129249.m: Income comes in, spending goes out.

a: Getting money from the flea market
129250.e: When you buy something, you spend money. That is called an expense.

129251.q: Tom has 4 francs. He gets another 6 francs of pocket money. How much does he have now?

129252.q: Why do many people take their money to the bank instead of keeping it under the bed?
a: Because it turns into more coins there
Because money is not allowed at home
129252.e: At home money can be stolen or burn. At the bank it is kept more safely.
129252.m: Money is better protected at the bank.

129253.q: You want to give your mum a present but you have little money. What is a good idea?
129253.e: Home-made presents cost little and often bring a lot of joy.
129253.m: A present does not have to be expensive.

129254.q: A chocolate bar costs 1 franc 20. You pay with 2 francs. How much do you get back?
129254.e: 2 francs are 200 centimes. 200 minus 120 makes 80 centimes.
129254.m: With centimes, work in small steps.

129255.q: Ida has three 5-franc coins and five 1-franc coins in her money box. How much money does she have?
129255.e: Three 5-franc coins are 15 francs, five 1-franc coins are 5 francs. Together that makes 20 francs.
129255.m: Count each kind of coin separately.

129256.q: At home you find a banknote on the table that is not yours. What do you do?
129256.e: Money that is not yours, you give back. That way others trust you.
129256.m: Other people’s money is given back.

129257.q: In a shop you see a toy you want straight away. What helps you avoid a bad buy?
a: Sleeping on it for a night
129257.e: Often the wish is smaller the next day. If you wait, you buy fewer things you later regret.

129258.q: Does the cash machine just give out money that does not belong to you?
a: No, it only gives money that is in your account
Yes, but only at the weekend
129258.e: The cash machine takes the money from your account. What you withdraw is then missing from the account.
129258.m: Money you withdraw is gone from your account.

129259.q: Three children share 9 francs equally. How much does each child get?
129259.e: 9 divided by 3 makes 3 francs for each child.
129259.m: Sharing fairly means the same for everyone.

129260.q: What saves your family money on water?
a: A short shower instead of a long bath
Leaving the water running while brushing your teeth
129260.e: Hot water needs energy and costs money. A short shower saves both.
129260.m: A short shower saves water and money.

129261.q: How can a child earn a little money with their parents’ permission?
a: Help the neighbour mow the lawn
129261.e: Small jobs like helping in the garden can add a bit to your pocket money. Your parents should know about it.

129262.q: Are you allowed to copy a banknote yourself and go shopping with it?
a: Yes, if the copy looks nice
129262.e: Copied money is counterfeit money. Shopping with it is forbidden and is punished.

129263.q: What is a good rule for your money box?
129263.e: If you save something regularly, even a little, you soon have a nice amount.

129264.q: A sign says “CHF 4.50”. How much does it cost?
129264.e: Before the point are the francs, after the point the centimes.
129264.m: Francs before the point, centimes after.

129265.q: What do the three letters “CHF” on a price tag mean?
129265.e: CHF is the abbreviation for the Swiss franc. You often see it on prices and bills.

129266.q: Mila gets 5 francs pocket money. She plans: save 2 francs, spend 3 francs. What is a plan like this called?
129266.e: A budget shows how you divide up your money. That way Mila knows exactly what she can spend.
129266.m: Dividing up money is called budgeting.

129267.q: Where is the best place to keep your money box?
a: In a safe place at home
On a seat on the bus
129267.e: In a safe place at home, your money box does not get lost.
129267.m: The money box stays in a safe place.

129268.q: Two woolly hats look the same. One costs 10 francs, the other 25 francs. What is smart?
a: Check whether the expensive one really is better
129268.e: Expensive does not always mean better. If you compare, you often save money.

129269.q: Why does a child usually get their first bank card together with their parents?
a: So the parents can help and keep an eye on things
Because children are not allowed money
Because otherwise the card does not light up
Because the parents keep the money
129269.e: With your first card you learn how to handle money. Your parents explain how to use it safely.
129269.m: Your first card comes with your parents’ help.

129270.q: Which note is worth the most?
129270.e: Of these four notes, the 200-franc note has the highest value.
129270.m: The number on the note shows its value.

129271.q: You have a 10-franc note and two 5-franc coins. How much money do you have?

129272.q: Lou saves 5 francs every month. How much does she have after 4 months?
129272.m: Month by month your savings grow.

129273.q: Apart from saving and spending, what else can you do with your own money?
a: Share or donate part of it
129273.e: Many children divide their money into three parts: saving, spending and helping others.

129274.q: A child in the playground wants your pocket money and threatens you. What do you do?
a: Tell a teacher or your parents straight away
129274.e: Nobody is allowed to take your money or threaten you. Adults will help you.
129274.m: If threatened, get help straight away.

129275.q: What goes on one side of a budget, and what on the other?
129275.e: A budget compares what comes in with what goes out. That shows whether the money is enough.

129276.q: Which expense is more likely to be a variable cost?
a: Money for the cinema and going out
129276.e: Variable costs change from month to month. You decide yourself how often you go to the cinema.
129276.m: You can control variable costs yourself.

129277.q: A budget shows more expenses than income. What is that called?
129277.e: With a deficit, money is missing. You have to cut expenses or bring in more.

129278.q: At the end of the month Elin has 40 francs left over. What is that called in a budget?
129278.e: A surplus is money left over after all expenses. You can save it, for example.
129278.m: What is left over is a surplus.

129279.q: Noah gets 60 francs a month. He spends 25 francs on his phone and 20 francs on snacks. How much can he save?
129279.e: 25 plus 20 makes 45 francs of expenses. 60 minus 45 makes 15 francs.
129279.m: Income minus expenses gives what is left.

129280.q: Which Swiss organisation gives guidelines on how much pocket money suits which age?
129280.e: Budget Counselling Switzerland publishes recommendations for pocket money and sample budgets for families.

129281.q: Luca, aged 15, wants to take out a mobile phone contract. What does he usually need?
129281.e: Minors can usually only sign contracts like this with regular costs if their parents agree.
129281.m: Under 18, a contract usually needs your parents.

129282.q: Why should you read the small print before clicking “Order”?
a: It often contains important costs and conditions
Because the prize is written there
129282.e: The small print shows, for example, the contract length, the notice period and the price. If you read it, you get fewer surprises.

129283.q: A streaming subscription is no longer being used. What is the smartest thing to do?
a: Delete the app and hope it stops
129283.e: If you only delete the app, you keep paying. Only cancelling ends the subscription.
129283.m: Cancel subscriptions you do not use.

129284.q: A jumper costs 50 francs. There is a 20% discount. How much does it cost now?
129284.e: 20% of 50 francs is 10 francs. 50 minus 10 makes 40 francs.
129284.m: Work out the discount, then subtract it.

129285.q: Trainers cost 80 francs, and in the sale there is 25% off. How much do you save?
129285.e: 25% is a quarter. A quarter of 80 francs is 20 francs.

129286.q: What is the price per kilo or per litre on many price tags for?
a: To compare packs of different sizes
To show the weight of the till
129286.e: Big packs are not always cheaper. The price per kilo shows what is really cheaper.
129286.m: Comparing per kilo shows the real price.

129287.q: Four friends eat pizza costing 48 francs altogether and share the bill equally. How much does each pay?
129287.m: Total divided by the number of people.

129288.q: Mara has 200 francs in her savings account and gets 2% interest a year. How much interest does she get?
129288.e: 1% of 200 francs is 2 francs. So 2% is 4 francs.

129289.q: What does a debit on a bank statement mean?
a: Money was taken from the account
The bank is giving money away
129289.e: A debit is a payment that leaves the account, for example a purchase made with a card.

129290.q: Why can you often only withdraw up to a certain maximum per day at a cash machine?
a: For protection in case the card is stolen
Because the machine never has enough money
Because the bank wants to save money
129290.e: The limit restricts the damage if a stranger uses the card. You can change it at the bank.

129291.q: Many banking apps let you block your card for certain countries. Why is that useful?
a: Fraudsters cannot use the card there
The card then stops working altogether
129291.e: If you only pay in Switzerland, you can block other countries. Stolen card details are then useless to fraudsters there.
129291.m: Blocking countries you do not need protects your card.

129292.q: How can you often spot a fake online shop?
a: Very low prices and payment in advance only
129292.e: Fake shops lure you with prices that are too good to be true and want the money first. The goods never arrive.

129293.q: Your banking app asks you to confirm an online payment. But you are not buying anything. What do you do?
a: Reject it and inform the bank
Send the code to a friend
129293.e: A request like this shows that someone is using your card details. If you reject it, the payment does not go through.
129293.m: Only confirm what you are doing yourself.

129294.q: What does a phishing message usually want from you?
129294.e: In phishing, fraudsters “fish” for login details. They want to get at your money with them.

129295.q: An email looks as if it is from your bank. What do you check first?
129295.e: Fraudsters often use similar but fake addresses. A close look shows a lot. If in doubt, ask the bank directly.

129296.q: What will your real bank never do?
a: Ask for your password by email
Answer your questions at the counter
129296.e: Reputable banks never ask for your password or PIN by email, text message or phone.
129296.m: The bank never asks for your password.

129297.q: A text message says: “Your parcel is waiting. Pay a 2-franc fee using this link.” What is this probably?
129297.e: Fraudsters use small amounts to get your card details. Afterwards they take much more.
129297.m: Do not open links in unexpected text messages.

129298.q: Someone wants you to pay a bill with gift card codes. What is true?
a: That is the safest way to pay
That is how the police do it
129298.e: Reputable companies and authorities never want to be paid with gift cards. Once the codes are passed on, the money is gone.
129298.m: Paying with gift cards is a warning sign.

129299.q: What happens in the so-called grandchild scam?
a: A caller pretends to be a relative and urgently wants money
129299.e: Fraudsters often call older people and claim a relative is in trouble. Then they ask for money.
129299.m: If asked for money on the phone, call back and check.

129300.q: A caller says he is from the police and wants to collect money or jewellery to keep it safe. What is true?
a: The real police never do anything like this
You should get it ready straight away
You must tell the bank and then hand it over
129300.e: The police never collect money or valuables from people’s homes. Call the emergency number 117 yourself.

129301.q: You are selling your old bike online. A buyer sends too much money “by mistake” and wants the rest back. What is this?
129301.e: Often the first payment was fake or is taken back later. If you send the rest back, you lose your own money.
129301.m: Overpaid and want the rest back? Be careful!

129302.q: Why should you never show a photo of your bank card on social media?
a: Others can misuse the card details
Because the bank charges for it
129302.e: The card shows the number and expiry date. Fraudsters can use them to shop online.
129302.m: Never photograph and share your cards.

129303.q: Why is online banking on open Wi-Fi in a café risky?
a: Strangers could read the data traffic
Because the Wi-Fi is too fast
129303.e: Open networks are often poorly protected. For banking it is better to use your own mobile network or your Wi-Fi at home.

129304.q: Why should you always update your phone and banking app?
a: Because otherwise the phone gets heavier
So the bank has fewer fees
129304.e: Updates fix flaws that fraudsters could exploit.

129305.q: A stranger sends you a link to an app that is not in the official app store. What do you do?
a: Send it to all your friends
Enter your password in the app
129305.e: Apps from unknown sources can contain malware that steals passwords.
129305.m: Only get apps from the official store.

129306.q: An online shop offers “Buy now, pay later”. What is the risk?
a: You lose track and reminder fees can follow
You get the money back twice
129306.e: If you pay later, it is easy to spend more than you have. If you pay too late, extra costs are added.

129307.q: A bill says “payable within 30 days”. What does that mean?
a: You must have paid it within 30 days at the latest
You may only pay after 30 days
129307.e: The payment period says by when the money should reach the recipient.
129307.m: The deadline says by when you must pay.

129308.q: Why do you keep the receipt for new headphones?
a: You need it for a warranty claim
Because otherwise you have to pay for it
129308.e: If something breaks during the warranty, the receipt proves when and where you bought it.
129308.m: Keep the receipt for the warranty.

129309.q: In Switzerland, does a shop have to take back a jumper in perfect condition just because you no longer like it?
a: Yes, but only with the label
129309.e: If the goods are fine, there is no right to an exchange. Many shops still do it as a goodwill gesture.
129309.m: Exchanges are usually a goodwill gesture by the shop.

a: Money you borrow and pay back later
Money you are given as a present
129310.e: With a loan, someone lends money. Often it is agreed when and with what interest it comes back.

129311.q: Which rule helps most to avoid getting into debt?
a: Only spend what you really have
Take out a loan every month
129311.e: If you do not spend more than you have, you do not need to borrow money.
129311.m: Do not spend more than you have.

129312.q: In this example, 1 franc gets you 1 euro. How many euros do you get for 50 francs?
129312.e: If 1 franc makes 1 euro, 50 francs are exactly 50 euros.
129312.m: The exchange rate tells you how much you get.

129313.q: What was money like in Switzerland before there was one franc for the whole country?
a: Many cantons and towns had their own coins
There was no money at all
129313.e: Before 1850 there were a great many kinds of coin in Switzerland. That made trade complicated.
129313.m: In the past almost every canton had its own money.

129314.q: Why can you shop with a paper banknote even though the paper itself is worth little?
a: Because everyone trusts that it has the value printed on it
Because it is made of gold
Because the bank swaps every note for chocolate
129314.e: Money works because people trust it. The Swiss National Bank makes sure the franc stays stable.

129315.q: Which image is found on all notes of the current Swiss banknote series?
129315.e: Hands are shown on every note of the current series. They stand for qualities of Switzerland.
129315.m: All the new notes show hands.

129316.q: Apart from the hands, what else can be seen on every note of the current series?
129316.e: The globe appears on all notes of the current series. It stands for Switzerland’s connection with the world.
129316.m: Every new note has a globe.

129317.q: Who is shown on the Swiss 5-franc coin?
a: The head of an Alpine herdsman
129317.e: The 5-franc coin shows the head of an Alpine herdsman. Many people wrongly think it is William Tell.
129317.m: The 5-franc coin shows an Alpine herdsman.

129318.q: Every month Lars gets a slip showing his gross pay, deductions and net pay. What is it called?
129318.e: The payslip shows how much you have earned and what has been deducted.

129319.q: What is it called when you move money from your current account to your own savings account?
129319.e: A transfer moves money between your own accounts, often with a few clicks in online banking.
129319.m: Transfer: moving money between your own accounts.

129320.q: Why does the bank ask for your ID when you open an account?
a: It has to know who you really are
Because it wants to collect your photo
Because otherwise the account turns red
129320.e: Banks have to know their customers. This protects against fraud and money laundering.
129320.m: The bank has to know who you are.

129321.q: One account is free, the other costs 5 francs a month. How much difference is that per year?
129321.e: 12 months times 5 francs makes 60 francs a year.

129322.q: Which trick helps against impulse buying online?
a: Leaving the basket for a day
Saving your card details in the shop
129322.e: If you wait a day, you often realise you do not need the thing at all.
129322.m: A day’s pause prevents bad buys.

129323.q: Why do you often see adverts online for things you looked at recently?
a: Because the bank shows them to you
129323.e: Many sites collect data about your browsing. That way they show adverts meant to tempt you to buy.
129323.m: Online adverts are tailored to you.

129324.q: A card terminal shows a higher amount than expected. What do you do before holding your card to it?
a: Hold the card to it twice
129324.e: Whatever you confirm is charged. A wrong amount is much easier to correct beforehand.

129325.q: What can happen if you leave your debit card in a shop and someone finds it?
a: They could make small contactless payments with it
Nothing, without the PIN nothing works
The bank notices at once and pays you everything
129325.e: Small contactless amounts often work without a PIN. That is why you block a lost card straight away.
129325.m: Block a lost card straight away.

129326.q: What is sensible for your bank card before a trip abroad?
a: Check whether the card is activated there
Write the PIN on the card
Leave the card at home and borrow cash
Give the card to a friend
129326.e: Some cards are blocked for certain countries. Checking in the app beforehand saves trouble.

129327.q: An influencer promises: “With my trick you will be rich in a week!” What do you think?
a: That is very hard to believe
I have to join in straight away
I will give him my savings account
129327.e: There is no such thing as quick money without risk. Promises like this are often advertising or a scam.
129327.m: Getting rich quick is a warning sign.

129328.q: Why does a debt with interest grow over time if you pay nothing back?
a: Because interest is added every year
Because the bank gives money away
129328.e: Interest is charged on borrowed money. If you pay nothing back, the amount keeps growing.

129329.q: What can happen if you do not pay bills for a long time?
a: Debt enforcement proceedings (Betreibung) can be started against you
129329.e: In debt enforcement, the creditor demands their money through the debt enforcement office. This can cause problems later, for example when looking for a flat.
129329.m: Unpaid bills can lead to debt enforcement.

129330.q: Where can a family get help if they can no longer pay their debts?
a: From a loan offer on the internet
129330.e: Debt advice centres help make a plan. A new loan usually makes the problem bigger.
129330.m: With debts, get advice, not a new loan.

129331.q: Why is gambling not a good way to make money grow?
a: You usually lose more than you win
129331.e: Gambling games are designed so that the operator makes money. In the long run the players lose.
129331.m: In gambling, the operator usually wins.

129332.q: What are loot boxes in games?
a: Surprise packs whose contents you do not know in advance
129332.e: You pay for a box and do not know what is inside. It is similar to gambling and can get expensive.

129333.q: Why do many games show prices in gems instead of francs?
a: So you notice less how much real money you are spending
129333.e: A game currency hides the real price. So it is better to work out what something costs in francs.

129334.q: Selin earns 500 francs in a holiday job. She saves 10%. How much is that?
129334.e: 10% is a tenth. A tenth of 500 francs is 50 francs.

129335.q: What does the saving tip “Pay yourself first” mean?
a: Save an amount right at the start of the month
Only look at what is left at the end of the month
129335.e: If you put your savings aside straight away, you do not spend them by accident.

129336.q: Why are children usually not allowed a real credit card?
a: Because you can get into debt with it
Because the card is too big
Because you only need it abroad
129336.e: With a credit card you pay first and only later with a bill. That can lead to debt.
129336.m: Credit card means buy first, pay later.

129337.q: Your bank statement shows a payment you do not recognise. What do you do?
a: Wait and see if there are more
Give the card to a friend
129337.e: An unknown payment can be fraud. The sooner the bank knows, the sooner it can help.

129338.q: An email from “your bank” has lots of mistakes and a strange greeting. What does that show?
a: The bank has a new style
It comes from the National Bank
129338.e: Phishing emails are often badly translated or do not address you by name.
129338.m: Lots of mistakes are a warning sign.

129339.q: A bank “support agent” contacts you in a chat and wants your login details. What do you do?
a: Reveal nothing and contact the bank on its official number
Send a photo of your card
Pass on the code from the app
129339.e: Real staff never ask for passwords. Fraudsters like to pretend to be support.
129339.m: Real support never asks for passwords.

129340.q: Someone promises you money if you give them your account details and online banking login. What is true?
a: That is fraud, never take part
That is a good side job
That is safe if he is nice
129340.e: If you let others use your account, you can get mixed up in crimes and lose money.
129340.m: Never let others use your account.

129341.q: Lia is looking for her first account. What should she compare?
a: Only the colour of the card
Only the name of the bank
129341.e: Fees for the account and card as well as a good app make everyday life easier and cheaper.
129341.m: Compare accounts by cost and usefulness.

129342.q: What is not one of the usual tasks of a commercial bank?
129342.e: In Switzerland only the National Bank issues banknotes. Commercial banks run accounts, grant loans and process payments.
129342.m: Only the National Bank issues notes.

129343.q: Roughly how many cantonal banks are there in Switzerland?
129343.e: Almost every canton has its own cantonal bank, 24 in total.
129343.m: Almost every canton has a cantonal bank.

129344.q: Why can it be cheaper to pay abroad by card instead of with cash exchanged beforehand?
a: Because bureaux de change often have poor rates and fees
129344.e: When exchanging money, providers earn from the rate and fees. Cards also cost something, so it is worth comparing.

129345.q: Why is the rate at which the bank sells euros higher than the rate at which it buys them?
a: The bank earns from the difference
129345.e: There is a spread between the buying and selling rate. The bank uses it to cover its costs and make money.
129345.m: When exchanging money, the bank earns from the spread.

129346.q: Why is the balance in the app sometimes not right straight after a card purchase?
a: Some payments are only booked after a few days
Because the bank gives the money away
129346.e: Card payments are often reserved first and only booked finally later.

129347.q: The Moser family wants a dog. Which costs come up regularly?
129347.e: An animal does not only cost money when you buy it. Food, the vet and insurance come up every year.
129347.m: A pet costs money all the time.

129348.q: How can you often save when shopping at the supermarket?
129348.e: Shops’ own brands are often cheaper and still of good quality.

129349.q: Mia expects to pay 1200 francs in tax a year. How much should she put aside each month?
129349.e: 1200 francs divided by 12 months makes 100 francs a month. That way the money is there when the bill arrives.

129350.q: What are provisions for in a personal budget?
a: For expenses that do not come every month, such as tax or the dentist
129350.e: Irregular expenses are spread across all months. That way they do not upset the budget.

129351.q: Luca receives a 13th month’s salary. What is the best way to include it in his budget?
a: Divide the annual salary by 12 and plan monthly with that
129351.e: If you spread the annual salary over 12 months, you have a realistic monthly amount and reserves for big bills.
129351.m: Spread the annual salary over 12 months.

129352.q: According to a common recommendation, roughly how big should an emergency fund be?
a: Three to six months of expenses
129352.e: With three to six months of expenses you can bridge, for example, a period of unemployment or a big repair.

129353.q: Why does the deductible (Franchise) belong in the budget as well as the premium?
a: Because you have to pay it yourself for medical costs
Because it is debited every month
129353.e: Up to the amount of the deductible, you pay medical costs yourself. Money should be ready for this.

129354.q: Nina takes out a loan of 5000 francs at 10% interest for one year. Roughly how much interest does she pay if she pays everything back at once at the end?
129354.e: 10% of 5000 francs is 500 francs. That is how much extra the loan costs.

129355.q: What does it mean to act as guarantor for a friend’s loan?
a: You are liable if she does not pay it back
You become the owner of the bank
You never have to pay anything
129355.e: A guarantor promises to pay the debt if the borrower cannot. That can get expensive.
129355.m: Being a guarantor means being liable.

a: The ability and willingness to repay debts
The number of accounts a person has
129356.e: Banks and landlords check creditworthiness to estimate their risk. Unpaid bills make it worse.

129357.q: Apart from savings, where else may the equity for an owner-occupied home come from in some cases?
129357.e: For owner-occupied property you can withdraw pension fund assets early or pledge them. But part of the equity must come from other sources.
129357.m: Pension fund money is possible for your own home.

129358.q: What is a capital gain on a share?
a: The profit when you sell a share for more than you paid
A prize in a language course
The interest on a savings account
129358.e: If the price of a share rises after you buy it, you make a capital gain when you sell.
129358.m: Capital gain: selling for more than you paid.

129359.q: How are private capital gains from shares taxed in Switzerland as a rule?
a: They are tax-free for private individuals
They are only taxed in Geneva
They must be given to the bank
129359.e: Profits from selling securities held as private assets are tax-free as a rule. Dividends, however, are income and are taxed.
129359.m: Private capital gains are tax-free, dividends are not.

129360.q: Why is it worth paying attention to the ongoing charges of funds?
a: Because high charges greatly reduce returns over the years
Because they make the risk disappear
129360.e: Even one per cent more in charges per year adds up to a lot of money over a long time.
129360.m: Low charges pay off in the long run.

129361.q: What is brokerage when trading securities?
a: A fee for each purchase or sale
129361.e: Banks and brokers charge a fee for every trade. So buying and selling often costs a lot.

129362.q: What do many banks charge a custody fee for?
129362.e: Securities are held in a custody account. Many banks charge a regular fee for running it.
129362.m: A custody account often costs a fee.

129363.q: What does liquidity mean for an investment?
a: How quickly you can turn it into cash
129363.e: Money in an account is very liquid. A house, on the other hand, cannot be sold quickly.

129364.q: What is one advantage of a monthly fund savings plan?
a: When prices are low you automatically buy more units
You get a fixed interest rate
129364.e: If you invest the same amount regularly, you get more units when prices are low. This smooths out the entry price.

129365.q: What happens if you lose the private key to your own crypto wallet?
a: You can usually never get at your funds again
The bank issues a new one
The National Bank replaces the money
129365.e: With cryptocurrencies there is no central body that can restore access. Without the key, the funds are lost.

a: A distributed ledger in which transactions are stored so they cannot be forged
A chain for locking your bike
129366.e: In a blockchain, data is stored in blocks and kept on many computers. Changing it afterwards is very hard.

129367.q: How does a Ponzi scheme work with investments?
a: Earlier investors are paid with new investors’ money
The money is invested in snow
The bank pays a fixed interest rate
129367.e: There are no real profits. As soon as no new investors join, the system collapses and most people lose their money.

129368.q: After an investment fraud, someone gets in touch offering to recover the lost money for a fee. What is this usually?
129368.e: Fraudsters deliberately target earlier victims. Anyone who pays loses even more money.
129368.m: Money back for a fee is often the next scam.

129369.q: Someone you met online but have never met in person asks for money for an emergency after weeks of chatting. What is likely?
a: A romance scam, so do not transfer any money
A real emergency, help at once
129369.e: In a so-called romance scam, fraudsters build up trust and then invent emergencies. The money is usually gone afterwards.
129369.m: Never send money to people you only know online.

129370.q: An email apparently from the boss asks the apprentice for an urgent, secret transfer. What is right?
a: Check with the boss through a known channel
Forward the email to everyone and then pay
129370.e: In CEO fraud, fraudsters pretend to be managers and put on pressure. Checking back through another channel uncovers the trick.

129371.q: A supplier says by email that their IBAN has changed. What do you do before the next payment?
a: Have it confirmed by phone on the known number
Use the new IBAN straight away
Reply to the email and ask if it is true
129371.e: Fraudsters often fake emails to redirect payments. A reply to the email may also end up with them.

a: Fraudsters have your phone number transferred to their SIM card
A discount on a phone contract
129372.e: That way fraudsters receive your text message codes. If your phone suddenly has no signal, you should contact your provider.
129372.m: Suddenly no signal? Call your provider straight away.

129373.q: What can a banking trojan do on a device?
a: Intercept login details and manipulate payments
129373.e: Malware like this often hides in unsafe apps or attachments. Updates and official stores protect you.

129374.q: An email with the subject “Your unpaid invoice” has a ZIP attachment from an unknown sender. What do you do?
a: Not open the attachment and delete the email
Forward it to all your contacts
Send your password as a reply
129374.e: Unexpected attachments can contain malware. You can check real invoices with the sender in another way.

129375.q: In a chat group, strangers urge everyone to buy a little-known share immediately. What is often behind this?
a: The organisers want to push the price up and then sell
A present from the stock exchange
129375.e: In a pump and dump, fraudsters buy early, push the price up with promotion and then sell. The others are left with losses.

129376.q: Your credit card statement shows a charge you do not recognise. What do you do?
a: Dispute it with the card issuer within the deadline
129376.e: You can dispute unauthorised charges with the card issuer. There are deadlines, so act quickly.

129377.q: A hotel reserves an amount on your credit card when you check in. What does that mean?
a: The amount is temporarily blocked but not yet paid
You have paid for the room twice
129377.e: The reservation covers possible costs. After checking out it is released or set against the real bill.
129377.m: A reservation is not yet a payment.

129378.q: What does the value date of a transaction show?
a: From when the amount counts for calculating interest
129378.e: The value date is the date the amount takes effect. It can differ from the booking date.
129378.m: The value date is when the amount takes effect.

129379.q: What does it mean to close out an account?
a: To close the account and pay out the balance
129379.e: When closing out, the balance is paid out or transferred and the account is closed. Standing orders should be changed beforehand.
129379.m: Closing out means closing the account.

129380.q: What is the reference number on a QR bill for?
a: So the recipient can match the payment to the right bill
129380.e: With the reference, the company automatically recognises which bill has been paid. That is why you should not change it.

a: A single payment area for euro transfers in Europe, which Switzerland also takes part in
129381.e: SEPA makes euro payments in Europe simple and cheap. Switzerland takes part in it.
129381.m: SEPA is the European euro payment area.

129382.q: In Switzerland, does a shopkeeper have to accept a bill paid entirely with 500 coins?
a: No, nobody has to accept more than 100 coins
129382.e: The law states that nobody is obliged to accept more than 100 circulation coins in one payment.
129382.m: Accepting at most 100 coins is required.

129383.q: What applies to Swiss banknotes of earlier series that are no longer in circulation?
a: They can be exchanged at the National Bank with no time limit
They can only be spent abroad
129383.e: Since 2020 the law no longer sets a deadline for exchanging recalled notes from the sixth series onwards.
129383.m: Old notes keep their value at the SNB.

129384.q: Which inscription is on the edge of the 5-franc coin?
129384.e: The edge of the 5-franc coin reads “DOMINUS PROVIDEBIT”, Latin for “The Lord will provide”, surrounded by stars.
129384.m: On the edge of the 5-franc coin: Dominus providebit.

129385.q: The franc becomes stronger against the euro. What usually happens?
a: Imports get cheaper, exports get more expensive for foreign buyers
Imports get more expensive, exports cheaper
129385.e: With a strong franc you can buy more in the euro area. But Swiss products become more expensive for customers abroad.
129385.m: Strong franc: cheap imports, expensive exports.

129386.q: The National Bank lowers its key interest rate. What usually happens to the interest on new loans?
129386.e: A lower key rate makes it cheaper for banks to get money. They often pass this on to borrowers.

129387.q: What does it mean that the National Bank is independent?
a: It decides on monetary policy without instructions from the government
It does not have to obey laws
129387.e: The Federal Constitution guarantees the SNB’s independence. That way monetary policy is not meant to depend on short-term political interests.
129387.m: The SNB is independent in monetary policy.

129388.q: Why do stricter rules apply to systemically important big banks?
a: Their collapse could endanger the whole economy
Because they belong to the National Bank
129388.e: This is called “too big to fail”. That is why such banks must hold more equity and have emergency plans.
129388.m: Too big to fail means stricter rules.

129389.q: How do your savings deposits appear on the bank’s balance sheet?
a: As the bank’s debts to you
129389.e: The bank owes you the money in your account. That is why customer deposits appear on the liabilities side of the balance sheet.
129389.m: For the bank, deposits are debts.

129390.q: How does a typical bank earn money in its interest business?
a: From the difference between loan interest and savings interest
129390.e: The bank pays savers little interest and charges borrowers more. The difference covers costs and brings profit.
129390.m: The interest margin is a core business of banks.

129391.q: What is part of a bank’s commission business?
a: Fees for securities trading and asset management
129391.e: Besides the interest business, banks earn fees for services such as stock market trading or advice.

a: Many customers withdraw their money at the same time because they distrust the bank
129392.e: Banks do not keep all deposits ready as cash. If everyone wants their money at the same time, the bank can get into difficulty.
129392.m: Bank run: everyone wants their money at once.

129393.q: Max wants to pay 50,000 francs in cash into his account. What will the bank probably do?
a: Ask where the money comes from
129393.e: With large or unusual amounts, banks have to check where the money comes from. This helps fight money laundering.

129394.q: What must a bank do if it has a well-founded suspicion of money laundering?
a: Report the case to the federal reporting office
129394.e: With a well-founded suspicion there is a duty to report to the Money Laundering Reporting Office. Banking secrecy does not protect crimes.
129394.m: Suspected money laundering must be reported.

129395.q: A phone costs 960 francs in cash or, on a contract, 24 instalments of 45 francs on top of the basic fee. How much more do the instalments cost?
129395.e: 24 times 45 francs makes 1080 francs. That is 120 francs more than the cash price.

a: A loan that lets you overdraw your account up to a limit
A savings account with fixed interest
129396.e: The bank allows a minus balance up to a certain amount. You usually pay high interest on the minus.
129396.m: Overdraft: overdrawing up to the limit.

129397.q: Why is it better to use your debit card rather than your credit card at a cash machine abroad?
a: Cash withdrawals with a credit card often cost more
Cash is free with the debit card
129397.e: Issuers often charge high fees for cash with a credit card. The debit card can cost something too, but usually less.
129397.m: Get cash with your debit card instead.

129398.q: Two friends open a joint account for their shared flat. What is important?
a: Clear agreements on who pays what and who may withdraw
That only one sees the balance
129398.e: Joint accounts easily lead to arguments. Clear rules help, for example for rent and shopping.
129398.m: A joint account needs clear rules.

129399.q: What changes in banking at the age of 18?
a: You can sign contracts such as loans on your own
You no longer have to pay fees
129399.e: When you come of age, you have full legal capacity. You then also bear full responsibility for debts.
129399.m: From 18 you decide yourself and are liable yourself.

129400.q: Can a 16-year-old apprentice generally decide for herself what to do with her apprentice wage?
a: Yes, she generally manages her earnings from work herself
No, it belongs entirely to her parents
129400.e: Under the Civil Code, a child manages their earnings from work themselves. If they live at home, a reasonable contribution to their keep can be asked for.
129400.m: You manage your own wage yourself.

129401.q: What is usually the safest way to pay when buying privately on online marketplaces?
a: Paying on collection after checking the goods
129401.e: If you only pay on handover, you see the goods first. Paying strangers in advance is a common route for fraud.
