129960.m: Low deductible: higher premium, earlier help.

129961.q: How can you save on the basic insurance premium without changing the deductible?
a: Choose a model such as Telmed or family doctor
Pay the premium only every other year
129961.e: If you give up free choice of doctor and first phone or see your family doctor, you usually pay a lower premium.

129962.q: In the Telmed model the advice line recommends seeing your family doctor. What is important?
a: Going straight to a specialist anyway
Calling again until you get a different answer
129962.e: In the Telmed model you have promised to follow the recommendations. Otherwise the insurer can reduce its payments.
129962.m: With Telmed you follow the recommendation.

129963.q: What do you tell the health insurer when you move house?
a: The names of the new neighbours
129963.e: The premium depends on where you live. After a move it may therefore go up or down.

129964.q: Sara moves from Zurich to Valais. What can happen to her health insurance premium?
a: It can change because the premium region changes
It will definitely stay the same
129964.e: Premiums differ by canton and region. A move can change the premium.
129964.m: A different place to live, a different premium.

129965.q: After a bee sting someone can hardly breathe and their face swells up. What do you do?
a: Put on a plaster and walk on
129965.e: A severe allergic reaction can be life-threatening. Then the ambulance service is needed immediately.
129965.m: Breathing problems after a sting: call 144 at once.

129966.q: In a case of poisoning, what should you not do unless Tox Info Suisse advises it?
129966.e: Vomiting can cause extra damage to the gullet and lungs. You call 145 and follow the instructions.
129966.m: With poisoning, do not make someone vomit.

129967.q: Tim sprains his ankle in PE. What helps first?
a: Rest, cool, bandage and raise it
Bathe the foot in hot water
129967.e: Rest, cooling, a light compression bandage and raising the foot reduce swelling and pain. If the pain is severe, you see a doctor.

129968.q: Which of these insurances is optional?
129968.e: Basic health insurance, AHV and motor vehicle liability insurance are required by law. Travel insurance is taken out voluntarily.

129969.q: Lina has paid a doctor's bill herself. What does she send to the health insurer?
a: The reimbursement copy of the bill
129969.e: With the reimbursement copy the insurer knows what it has to pay back. Many insurers also accept it via an app.
129969.m: Submit the copy to get reimbursed.

129970.q: After a serious accident abroad, what can travel insurance organise and pay for?
a: A new hotel room on the beach
129970.e: Transport home, by air ambulance for example, is very expensive. Basic insurance usually does not pay for it, but travel insurance does.

129971.q: Where does the European Health Insurance Card help?
a: In the EU and EFTA countries
129971.e: The European Health Insurance Card is valid in the EU and the EFTA countries. Outside Europe you often need travel insurance.
129971.m: The European card is valid in the EU and EFTA.

129972.q: When does an apprentice need a doctor's certificate for the training company?
a: When she is off sick for several days
129972.e: The doctor's certificate confirms that you cannot work. From when it is needed is stated in the company's contract or rules.
129972.m: Longer illness needs a doctor's certificate.

129973.q: What do some health insurers offer if you pay the premium for the whole year in advance?
129973.e: For paying in advance some insurers give a small discount. But you need to have the whole amount at once.
129973.m: Paying yearly sometimes brings a discount.

129974.q: Depending on the contract, what does supplementary outpatient insurance often contribute to?
129974.e: Supplementary insurance pays for services that basic insurance does not cover, or only partly. Exactly what is stated in the contract.
129974.m: The contract says what supplementary insurance pays.

129975.q: Mia works 30 hours a week for three weeks in the summer holidays. How is she insured against free-time accidents during this period?
129975.e: Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer is also insured against free-time accidents through the employer.
129975.m: From 8 hours a week the employer also covers free-time accidents.

129976.q: During a thunderstorm water gets into the cellar and your own bikes go rusty. What kind of damage is this?
129976.e: Flooding after a storm counts as natural hazard damage. Household contents insurance then pays for your own things.
129976.m: Storm water is natural hazard damage.

129977.q: After a fire the flat can no longer be lived in. What does household contents insurance often also pay for?
a: New school books for all the children in the municipality
129977.e: Many contents policies also pay extra costs, for a hotel for example, until you can return to the flat. The details are in the policy.
129977.m: Contents insurance can also pay temporary costs.

129978.q: Why should you always report damage to the insurer truthfully?
a: False information can lead to losing the payment
Because otherwise it takes longer, but it does not matter
Because otherwise the insurer pays more
Because then you get a reward
129978.e: Lying in a claim report is insurance fraud. The insurer can then refuse to pay and cancel the contract.

129979.q: What is especially important when calling the Rega in the mountains?
a: Giving your exact location, for example with the Rega app
The name of the hotel from your last holiday
129979.e: The Rega can land almost anywhere. What matters is that it knows the exact spot; the Rega app sends it automatically.
129979.m: The exact location matters for the rescue.

129980.q: Why do some people with an illness or allergy carry an emergency card?
a: So helpers have important information in an emergency
So they can travel free by train
129980.e: Someone with diabetes or a severe allergy, for example, may not be able to speak in an emergency. A card informs the rescuers.
129980.m: An emergency card speaks when you cannot.

129981.q: What is a cost approval from the health insurer?
a: The promise to pay for a particular treatment
129981.e: For some expensive treatments the doctor asks the insurer beforehand. With the cost approval you know the insurer will pay.
129981.m: The cost approval says in advance: the insurer pays.

129982.q: Why is it worth collecting insurance documents in a folder?
a: You can quickly find the policy, statements and bills
Because otherwise the insurer will not pay
129982.e: When there is damage or a question, you need the right papers quickly. A folder, or a digital folder, helps.

129983.q: What does it mean if someone causes damage through gross negligence?
a: They were very careless and could easily have prevented it
129983.e: Gross negligence means ignoring the most basic safety rules. Then an insurer can reduce its payment.
129983.m: Gross negligence can reduce the payment.

129984.q: Mrs Bühler leaves a burning candle unattended and goes out. A fire breaks out. What can the contents insurance do?
a: Reduce the payment because of gross negligence
129984.e: Leaving a candle burning unattended is often regarded as gross negligence. The insurer may then pay less, depending on the contract.

129985.q: Elias deliberately smashes a window. Does his liability insurance pay?
a: No, deliberate damage is not insured
129985.e: Insurers do not pay for damage caused on purpose. Anyone who breaks something deliberately pays themselves and can be punished.

129986.q: While cleaning, cleaning product splashes into Paul's eye. What do you do immediately?
a: Rinse the eye with water for a long time
Nothing, it goes away by itself
129986.e: Chemicals in the eye are rinsed out immediately and for a long time with plenty of water. Then Tox Info Suisse on 145 or the doctor can advise.
129986.m: Chemicals in the eye: rinse at once, for a long time.

129987.q: What do you take on a trip if you need medicines regularly?
a: Enough medicine in the original pack
Just a few loose tablets in your trouser pocket
Nothing, you buy something on the way
129987.e: The same medicine may not be available abroad. And in the original pack it is clear what it is.
129987.m: Take medicines in their original pack.

129988.q: Mr Kunz is retired and falls while cleaning the windows. Which insurance pays for the treatment?
129988.e: Anyone who is no longer employed has no accident insurance through an employer. Then the health insurance with included accident cover pays.
129988.m: Without an employer, health insurance also covers accidents.

129989.q: Basic insurance does not pay for normal dental treatment. So what makes sense?
a: Going for regular check-ups so small problems are treated early
Only going when it hurts a lot
129989.e: Small holes are cheap to treat. Big problems discovered too late become much more expensive.

129990.q: Why is treatment at A&E usually more expensive than at the family doctor's surgery?
a: Experts and equipment are ready there around the clock
Because you do not need an insurance card there
129990.e: A&E is ready day and night for serious cases. That costs a lot, so with minor complaints it is better to see the family doctor.
129990.m: Minor complaints do not belong in A&E.

129991.q: What should you tell the pharmacy when you buy a new medicine?
a: Which other medicines you already take
Where you are going on holiday
129991.e: Some medicines do not go well together. The pharmacy can check this if it knows everything.
129991.m: Tell the pharmacy all your medicines.

129992.q: Why does the insurer often ask for police confirmation after a theft?
a: As proof that the theft was reported
So the police get the premium
Because the police replace the things
129992.e: The confirmation of the report shows that the theft really was reported. That is why you go to the police quickly after a theft.
129992.m: Always report a theft to the police.

129993.q: Water is dripping from a pipe in the kitchen. What should you do before the insurer comes?
a: Turn off the water and keep the damage as small as possible
Let it all run so you get more money
Leave the flat for a week
Touch nothing, not even turn off the water
129993.e: You are obliged to keep damage as small as possible. Turning off the water and taking photos is right.

129994.q: Where does it say how long a contents insurance contract runs and how to cancel it?
a: In the policy and the terms and conditions
129994.e: The term and the notice periods are in the policy and the general terms and conditions. You should read them before signing.

129995.q: What belongs in a travel first aid kit for a family holiday?
a: Plasters, fever medicine and your own medicines
A glass thermometer for each child
129995.e: On the road a pharmacy is not always open straight away. With a small travel kit you can treat simple complaints yourself.
129995.m: Pack a travel first aid kit for the holidays.

129996.q: When comparing contents insurance, what should you not look at alone?
a: The price; you also check cover and excess
The colour of the logo only
The length of the letters only
129996.e: The cheapest insurance is not always the best. What is covered, the sum insured and the excess also matter.
129996.m: Do not compare the price alone.

129997.q: At 18 Luca comes of age. What changes about his insurance?
a: He is responsible for his own contracts
He no longer needs health insurance
He may no longer have insurance
129997.e: Adults sign their own contracts and are responsible for bills. Even if the parents still pay, it is good to know your insurance.

129998.q: For which vehicle do you need a number plate with liability insurance?
a: A fast e-bike up to 45 km/h
129998.e: Fast e-bikes up to 45 km/h need a yellow number plate with liability insurance. Ordinary bikes and slow e-bikes do not.
129998.m: Fast e-bikes need a number plate.

129999.q: The health insurance premium bill is twice as high as usual. What do you do?
a: Ask and have the reason checked
129999.e: Perhaps two months were charged together, or there is a mistake. A quick question clears it up.

130000.q: What preventive care does basic insurance pay for children, even when they are healthy?
130000.e: Children have regular check-ups at which growth and development are monitored. Basic insurance helps pay for them.
130000.m: Basic insurance helps pay for children's check-ups.

130001.q: What does the basic rule of liability in the Code of Obligations (Art. 41 CO) state?
a: Anyone who unlawfully and culpably causes damage to another must compensate it
All damage is paid by the state
Only companies are liable for damage
Damage only has to be compensated if caused on purpose
130001.e: Art. 41 CO governs fault-based liability: there must be damage, an unlawful act, fault and a causal link. Even negligence is enough as fault.
130001.m: Whoever culpably causes harm must compensate it.

130002.q: Under the Code of Obligations, when is a dog owner not liable for damage caused by her dog?
a: If she proves she took all due care
If the damage happens at the weekend
Never, she is always fully liable
130002.e: Animal keeper's liability is strict liability: the keeper is liable even without fault. She can only escape it by proving she took the necessary care.
130002.m: Animal keepers are liable unless they prove due care.

130003.q: Under the Road Traffic Act, who is primarily liable for damage caused by a car in operation?
a: The registered keeper of the vehicle
Always the person in the passenger seat
The garage that sold the car
The canton that issues the number plate
130003.e: Motor vehicles are subject to strict keeper liability. That is why the keeper must take out motor vehicle liability insurance.
130003.m: The keeper is liable for the car.

130004.q: From whom can someone injured in a car accident claim money directly?
a: Directly from the vehicle's liability insurer
Only from the Federal Supreme Court
Only from their own health insurer
From the municipality where the accident happened
130004.e: In motor vehicle accidents, injured parties have a direct right of claim against the liability insurer. They do not first have to sue the keeper.
130004.m: Injured parties can go straight to the insurer.

130005.q: A driver causes an accident while drunk. The liability insurance pays the injured parties. What can it do afterwards?
a: Reclaim part of the money from the driver
130005.e: The insurer pays the injured parties in full. But in cases of gross negligence such as drink driving it takes recourse against the driver.
130005.m: Recourse means the insurer claims money back.

130006.q: Which damage does partial cover (Teilkasko) for a car typically include?
a: Theft, glass breakage, hail and marten damage
Damage to the car in a collision you caused
Damage to the other party's car
130006.e: Partial cover pays for damage to your own car from events such as theft, glass breakage, natural hazards or animals. Damage to the other party is paid by liability insurance.
130006.m: Partial cover: theft, glass, nature, animals.

130007.q: What does fully comprehensive cover pay in addition to partial cover?
a: Damage to your own car in an accident you caused
130007.e: Fully comprehensive (collision) cover also pays for damage to your own vehicle that you caused yourself. It is worthwhile mainly for newer cars.
130007.m: Fully comprehensive also pays for self-caused damage to your own car.

130008.q: What does a bonus mean in motor insurance?
a: A lower premium after claim-free years
A higher excess for young drivers
130008.e: If you make no claims for a long time, you move into a cheaper premium level. After a claim the premium can rise again.

130009.q: By law, what is the maximum rent deposit for a flat?
a: As much as the landlady wants
130009.e: The Code of Obligations allows at most three months' rent as security for flats. The money goes into a blocked account in the tenant's name.
130009.m: Rent deposit: at most three months' rent.

130010.q: When moving out Anna damages a 15-year-old carpet. Why does her liability insurance often pay only a little?
a: Because only the residual value after its lifespan is replaced
Because the landlady is to blame
130010.e: Fittings have standard lifespans. If a carpet is near the end of its lifespan, its residual value is small, and only that is replaced.
130010.m: Old fittings only have a small residual value.

130011.q: What determines whether a child is personally liable for damage it has caused?
130011.e: Anyone with capacity of judgement can assess the consequences of their actions and is in principle liable themselves. Small children often lack this.
130011.m: Liability depends on capacity of judgement.

130012.q: When can parents be liable for damage caused by their child?
a: If they did not exercise the required supervision
Never, only the child is liable
Only if the child is an adult
130012.e: The head of the family is liable for damage caused by children in the household unless they prove they took the usual and required care in supervising them.
130012.m: Parents are liable if they neglect supervision.

130013.q: Household contents are worth 100,000 francs but only 50,000 francs are insured. Water damage costs 10,000 francs. How much does the insurer pay, without excess?
130013.e: With underinsurance the insurer pays in proportion of sum insured to value, here half. Half of 10,000 francs is 5,000 francs.

130014.q: Household contents are usually insured at replacement value. What does that mean?
a: You receive the amount for a new item of equal quality
You receive the price you would get on a second-hand platform
You only receive the value on the day of purchase ten years ago
130014.e: With replacement value you are paid what an equivalent new item costs today. That is why the sum insured must also be based on replacement value.
130014.m: Replacement value means what it costs to buy new.

130015.q: What is the current value of an item?
a: The replacement value minus wear and tear
The value of the clock in the living room
The price in a hundred years
The time it took to buy it
130015.e: The current value takes age and wear into account. It is usually lower than the replacement value.
130015.m: Current value is replacement value minus wear.

130016.q: The same household contents are accidentally insured with two insurers. How much do you receive in total for damage of 3,000 francs?
130016.e: In indemnity insurance you may not profit. Even with double insurance the damage is only compensated once, so a double premium is pointless.

130017.q: Under the Insurance Contract Act, within what period can you withdraw from a new contract with a private insurer?
130017.e: Since the revision of the Insurance Contract Act there is a right of withdrawal of 14 days. The withdrawal must be made in writing or in another provable form.

130018.q: Paul has taken out household contents insurance for ten years. What does the Insurance Contract Act allow him?
a: He can cancel at the end of the third year
He must stay for all ten years
He can cancel any day without notice
He can only cancel if he moves
130018.e: Every insurance contract can be cancelled at the end of the third or any later year, regardless of the agreed term, with three months' notice.
130018.m: After three years you may cancel.

130019.q: With many private insurances, what may both sides do after a claim?
a: Tear up the policy and rewrite it
130019.e: After a claim the Insurance Contract Act allows both the insurer and the insured person to cancel the contract. For supplementary health insurance there is an exception for the insurer.
130019.m: After a claim, cancellation is possible.

130020.q: May a health insurer give regular notice on supplementary hospital insurance because a person causes high costs?
a: No, for supplementary health insurance it waives regular notice
130020.e: The Insurance Contract Act protects people with supplementary health insurance: the insurer may not give them regular notice. So you stay insured in old age or when ill.
130020.m: The insurer cannot give regular notice on supplementary health cover.

130021.q: What is risk equalisation between health insurers?
a: Insurers with many healthy members pay into insurers with many ill members
All insurers pay a tax to the Confederation
Ill people pay higher premiums than healthy ones
130021.e: Because all insurers must accept everyone, risk equalisation balances differences in age, sex and illness. That makes hunting for good risks less worthwhile.
130021.m: Risk equalisation balances costs between insurers.

130022.q: Who must approve basic health insurance premiums every year?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
130022.e: Health insurers submit their premiums to the FOPH. The office checks that they cover costs and are not excessive.
130022.m: The FOPH approves basic insurance premiums.

130023.q: What is the maximum number of premium regions a canton may have for basic insurance?
130023.e: A canton can be divided into up to three premium regions; smaller cantons often have only one. Cities usually have higher premiums than rural areas.
130023.m: At most three premium regions per canton.

130024.q: Besides the health insurer, who pays part of the costs of an inpatient stay in the general ward?
130024.e: Inpatient hospital treatment is split between the canton and the health insurer. The canton's share is funded by taxes.
130024.m: Canton and insurer share hospital costs.

130025.q: How are people receiving unemployment benefit insured against free-time accidents?
a: Through their last employer's liability insurance
130025.e: Anyone receiving unemployment benefit is compulsorily insured against accidents with Suva. The premium is deducted from the benefit.
130025.m: Unemployed people have accident cover through Suva.

130026.q: A recruit is injured during basic military training. Which insurance is responsible?
130026.e: During military service, civilian service and civil protection you are insured through military insurance. It pays for illnesses and accidents during that time.
130026.m: During military service, military insurance is responsible.

130027.q: What can you apply for in basic insurance during military service of more than 60 consecutive days?
a: Suspend the insurance and pay no premium
A switch to a private room
130027.e: Because military insurance is responsible during that time, you can suspend basic insurance. That saves premiums.
130027.m: Long military service: suspend basic insurance.

130028.q: After a job ends, how long do you remain insured against free-time accidents through the employer?
a: Until the 31st day after the end of the entitlement to wages
Not at all, cover ends immediately
130028.e: Non-occupational accident insurance continues for 31 days after the entitlement to wages ends. After that you need extension cover or the accident cover of your health insurance.
130028.m: After a job, 31 more days of accident cover.

130029.q: Which insurance pays for medical treatment of recognised congenital conditions up to the 20th birthday?
130029.e: For recognised congenital conditions the IV covers medical measures up to the age of 20. After that the health insurer is responsible.
130029.m: The IV pays for congenital conditions up to 20.

130030.q: Mrs Arnold works 40 hours a week. She has an accident on the way to work. How does this accident count?
130030.e: For people working at least 8 hours a week, an accident on the way to work counts as non-occupational. Only those who work less are covered on the way by occupational accident insurance.
130030.m: From 8 hours: the way to work is non-occupational.

130031.q: What are “accident-like injuries” under the Accident Insurance Act (UVG)?
a: Certain injuries, such as torn ligaments, that can be covered even without a clear accident
Damage to a car after an accident
130031.e: The UVG lists certain injuries, such as torn menisci or ligaments. Accident insurance pays for them unless they are mainly due to wear or illness.

a: An illness mainly caused by your work
An illness you only have on Mondays
An injury playing sport at the weekend
130032.e: Occupational diseases, caused by certain substances or noise at work for example, are covered by compulsory accident insurance.
130032.m: Accident insurance pays for occupational diseases.

130033.q: Claudia has a deductible (Franchise) of 1500 francs. Her costs for the year are 2000 francs. How much does she pay herself?
130033.e: She first pays the deductible of 1500 francs. Of the remaining 500 francs she bears a 10 per cent co-payment, so 50 francs.
130033.m: Deductible plus 10 per cent of the rest.

130034.q: Mr Imhof has a deductible (Franchise) of 500 francs and costs of 8000 francs in the year, without a hospital stay. How much does he pay himself?
130034.e: Deductible 500 francs, plus 10 per cent of 7500 francs, which is 750 francs. Because the co-payment is capped at 700 francs, he pays 500 plus 700 francs.
130034.m: The co-payment is capped at 700 francs.

130035.q: A child with a deductible (Franchise) of 300 francs has costs of 1000 francs in the year. How much do the parents pay?
130035.e: The parents pay the first 300 francs as the deductible. Of the remaining 700 francs, 10 per cent is added, so 70 francs.
130035.m: For children too: deductible plus 10 per cent.

130036.q: With a 2500 deductible (Franchise), Eva saves 1200 francs in premiums a year compared with a 300 deductible. She has costs of 5000 francs every year. Which is cheaper?
a: Deductible 300, she saves 780 francs in total
130036.e: With 300 she pays 300 plus 470 francs, so 770 francs herself. With 2500 it is 2500 plus 250, so 2750 francs. The difference of 1980 francs is larger than the premium saving of 1200 francs.
130036.m: With high costs the low deductible pays off.

130037.q: Besides the number of tax points, what determines the price of a single outpatient service at the doctor's?
a: The tax point value, which differs by canton
The weather on the day of treatment
The number of people in the waiting room
130037.e: Each service has a certain number of tax points. Multiplied by the tax point value this gives the price in francs, and this value is not the same everywhere.
130037.m: Tax points times tax point value gives the price.

130038.q: What is a payment order in debt collection proceedings?
a: The official demand from the debt collection office to pay a debt
A friendly reminder from the surgery
A court judgement imposing a penalty
A voucher from the health insurer
130038.e: If a bill is not paid despite reminders, the creditor can start debt collection. The debt collection office then serves the payment order.
130038.m: The debt collection office serves the payment order.

130039.q: What does an advance healthcare directive set out?
a: Which medical measures you want if you lose capacity of judgement
Which health insurer you choose next year
How high the premium may be
130039.e: In the advance directive you record which treatments you want or refuse in a situation where you cannot judge for yourself. Doctors must respect it.
130039.m: The advance directive speaks when you cannot.

130040.q: Under the Code of Obligations, for how long at least must an employer pay wages during illness in the first year of service, unless agreed otherwise?
130040.e: If the employment lasts more than three months, wages continue for three weeks in the first year of service. Many companies instead have better daily sickness allowance insurance.
130040.m: Legal minimum in the first year: three weeks.

130041.q: From when does compulsory accident insurance pay a daily allowance?
a: From the third day after the day of the accident
Only on the day of the accident
130041.e: The daily allowance starts on the third day after the day of the accident. For the first days the employer usually continues to pay wages.
130041.m: UVG daily allowance from the third day.

130042.q: Unlike compulsory accident insurance, what does health insurance not pay after an accident?
a: A daily allowance for lost wages
130042.e: The accident cover of health insurance pays treatment costs with deductible and co-payment. A daily allowance for lost wages is only available through accident insurance under the UVG.
130042.m: Wage replacement after an accident comes via the UVG.

130043.q: Why is natural hazard damage almost always included in household contents insurance in Switzerland?
a: Because by law it is linked to fire insurance
Because there are never storms in Switzerland
Because health insurance pays for it
Because it always has an extra premium of 0 francs
130043.e: Anyone who insures contents or a building against fire is automatically also insured against natural hazards such as floods, storms or hail.

130044.q: Which natural event is not included in the usual natural hazard cover?
130044.e: In Switzerland earthquakes do not count as an insured natural hazard under fire insurance. There are only special or voluntary covers for them.

130045.q: What applies to buildings insurance in many cantons?
a: A public cantonal institution compulsorily insures all buildings
130045.e: Many cantons have a cantonal buildings insurer with a monopoly. Homeowners there are automatically insured and pay a premium.
130045.m: Many cantons have their own buildings insurer.

130046.q: The glass ceramic hob in your own flat cracks. Which cover pays for it?
130046.e: Glass breakage is often an add-on to household contents insurance. It pays for cracked hobs, mirrors or glass tables, for example.
130046.m: Glass breakage is usually an add-on.

130047.q: Whom can you turn to free of charge in a dispute with your contents or liability insurer?
130047.e: There is a separate ombudsman for private insurance who mediates neutrally. The health insurance ombudsman's office deals with health insurers.
130047.m: Private insurance has its own ombudsman.

130048.q: A caller wants to sell Lea a new health insurance policy on the phone straight away. What is wise?
a: Sign nothing on the phone and compare offers in writing
Agree immediately so the offer does not expire
Give your insurance number and bank details
Cancel the old insurer the same day
130048.e: Under time pressure you make bad decisions. You ask for documents, compare neutrally, on Priminfo for example, and then decide.
130048.m: Never take out insurance on the phone under pressure.

130049.q: After debt collection over unpaid premiums, the health insurer receives a certificate of loss. What does that mean?
a: The debt could not be paid in full and still exists
A police certificate after a theft
130049.e: If not everything can be paid in a seizure, the creditor receives a certificate of loss. The debt remains and can be claimed again later.
130049.m: A certificate of loss means: debt not fully paid.

130050.q: May a health insurer tell an employer which illness an employee has?
a: No, health data is specially protected
Yes, if the premium is high
Yes, but only at the end of the year
130050.e: Health data counts as particularly sensitive. From a doctor's certificate the employer only learns whether and for how long someone cannot work, not the diagnosis.
130050.m: The diagnosis is none of the employer's business.

130051.q: Which number reaches Die Dargebotene Hand, the helpline that listens to adults with worries?
130051.e: Die Dargebotene Hand can be reached on 143 around the clock, in confidence. For children and young people there is 147.

130052.q: What does “prescribed by a doctor” mean?
a: A doctor has ordered the treatment or remedy
You chose it yourself in the shop
130052.e: Basic insurance only pays for many services, such as physiotherapy or certain medicines, if a doctor has prescribed them.
130052.m: Prescribed means ordered by the doctor.

130053.q: By how much at least must the cantons reduce the premiums of children from low and middle income households?
130053.e: The Health Insurance Act (KVG) requires a reduction of at least 80 per cent for children in low and middle income households. For young adults in education it is at least 50 per cent.
130053.m: Children's premiums: at least 80 per cent reduction.

130054.q: A person cannot pay their premiums, and debt collection ends with a certificate of loss. Who then covers a large part of the debt?
a: The canton of residence, 85 per cent
130054.e: For certificates of loss from basic insurance the canton covers 85 per cent of the claim. But that does not simply wipe out the person's debt.
130054.m: For certificates of loss the canton steps in with 85 per cent.

130055.q: By when can you tell your insurer that you want a higher deductible (Franchise) for the new year?
130055.e: For a lower deductible the deadline is 30 November, because that is treated like a cancellation. A higher deductible can be chosen until the end of the year, starting 1 January.
130055.m: Higher deductible: tell them by the end of the year.

130056.q: Under what condition can you deduct self-paid medical costs from direct federal tax?
a: Insofar as they exceed 5 per cent of net income
130056.e: Medical costs you bear yourself, such as the deductible and co-payment, can be deducted federally insofar as they exceed 5 per cent of net income. So you should keep the receipts.
130056.m: High own medical costs can lower your tax.

130057.q: Lukas wants to have a planned operation abroad by choice. What does basic insurance pay in principle?
a: Nothing, planned treatments abroad are usually not covered
130057.e: Abroad, basic insurance mainly pays for emergencies. Anyone who deliberately has treatment abroad usually pays for it themselves or needs suitable supplementary insurance.
130057.m: Basic insurance usually does not pay for planned treatment abroad.

130058.q: Which three criteria must basic insurance services meet?
130058.e: The KVG requires services to be effective, appropriate and economical, known as WZW. This is reviewed regularly.

130059.q: What is the job of a health insurer's medical adviser (Vertrauensarzt)?
a: He examines medical questions for the insurer and is bound by confidentiality
He treats all members at home
130059.e: Medical advisers assess, for example, whether a service must be paid for. They pass on only the necessary information to the administration.
130059.m: The medical adviser examines medical questions for the insurer.

130060.q: What does the principle “outpatient before inpatient” mean?
a: Certain procedures should be done without an overnight stay if medically possible
You must always go to hospital first
Ambulances have priority on the road
130060.e: For a list of procedures, basic insurance in principle only pays if they are done as outpatient treatment. There are exceptions where medical reasons speak against it.
130060.m: Outpatient instead of inpatient where possible.

130061.q: What is a second opinion before a major operation?
a: Another doctor's assessment of the same question
A review of the hospital kitchen
130061.e: For important decisions a second expert can help find the best treatment. Many insurers explicitly support this.
130061.m: A second opinion helps before major procedures.

130062.q: Does the employer's compulsory accident insurance also apply to a skiing accident on holiday in Austria?
a: Yes, in principle it applies worldwide
Only with a permit from the canton
130062.e: Non-occupational accident insurance in principle also applies abroad. For very expensive countries, travel insurance can still make sense.

130063.q: Since the revision of the Therapeutic Products Act, what may pharmacists do in certain cases?
a: Supply some prescription-only medicines without a doctor's prescription after a personal consultation
Sign doctor's certificates for training companies
130063.e: For certain medicines and uses, pharmacists may supply them without a doctor's prescription after a consultation. This is documented.
130063.m: Pharmacies may supply some things without a prescription.

130064.q: Why is it important for everyone that insured people check their doctor's bills?
a: Wrongly charged services raise costs and therefore premiums
Because otherwise you get no insurance card
Because you get a bonus from the Confederation
130064.e: Insurers check bills too, but only the patient knows exactly what was done. Every corrected mistake relieves the premium payers.
130064.m: Checking bills helps all premium payers.

130065.q: Why does it make sense to ask an insurance adviser how she is paid?
a: She often receives a commission from the insurer whose products she sells
Because she is paid by the canton
130065.e: A commission can influence the advice. If you know how someone earns, you can judge recommendations better and compare neutrally.
130065.m: Ask about commission when getting advice.

130066.q: Roughly how many times per minute do you press during chest compressions on an adult?
130066.e: You press hard and fast, about 100 to 120 times a minute, in the middle of the chest. A defibrillator complements the compressions.

130067.q: How deep should an adult's chest be pressed down during chest compressions?
a: Not at all, you only stroke it
130067.e: Only with enough depth is blood pumped round the body. After each push you let the chest come fully back up.

130068.q: If you also give rescue breaths during resuscitation, what is the ratio of compressions to breaths for an adult?
130068.e: The recommendation is 30 compressions and 2 breaths. Anyone who cannot or will not give breaths keeps pressing without a break.

130069.q: A man with diabetes suddenly seems confused and is shaking, but is awake and can swallow. What helps as first aid?
a: Give sugar or a sugary drink
Give a glass of water without sugar
Let him sleep and do nothing
130069.e: These are typical signs of low blood sugar. Sugar helps quickly; if it does not get better or the person stops responding, you call 144.
130069.m: Low blood sugar in an awake person: give sugar.

130070.q: Why does every minute count when a stroke is suspected?
a: Because brain cells die with every minute without treatment
Because the health insurer only pays on the same day
130070.e: In a stroke part of the brain no longer gets blood. The faster the treatment in hospital, the less lasting damage.

130071.q: How much does basic insurance pay towards medically necessary rescue costs in Switzerland, after a mountain accident for example?
a: 50 per cent, at most 5000 francs a year
130071.e: For rescues in Switzerland basic insurance pays half, up to a maximum of 5000 francs a year. Other insurances cover the rest, or you pay yourself.
130071.m: Rescue: 50 per cent, up to 5000 francs.

130072.q: For how many sessions at most is a doctor's order for psychological psychotherapy valid?
130072.e: One order is valid for a maximum of 15 sessions. Further sessions need a new order, and after a certain number also a review with the insurer.
130072.m: One order covers up to 15 sessions.

130073.q: What does basic insurance not pay for during a stay in a care home?
130073.e: Basic insurance contributes to the care costs. Residents pay for accommodation and food themselves, with supplementary benefits if needed.
130073.m: In a care home you pay for housing and food yourself.

130074.q: What is the electronic patient record?
a: A voluntary digital collection of important health documents
A compulsory app for all children
The list of all premiums in Switzerland
An online shop of the pharmacies
130074.e: Reports, medication lists or vaccinations can be stored in the electronic patient record. The patient decides who may access it.
130074.m: In the patient record the patient controls access.

130075.q: What distinguishes burglary from simple theft?
a: The thief forces their way into a locked space
In burglary only money is stolen
Simple theft only happens at night
130075.e: If a door is forced or a window smashed, it is called burglary. If a bike is taken from the street, for example, it is simple theft.
130075.m: Burglary means forcing your way in.

130076.q: What does household contents insurance call robbery?
a: Theft with violence or the threat of violence
A phone forgotten on the train
130076.e: If someone's bag is snatched by force or they are threatened, that is robbery. Many contents policies also cover it away from home.

130077.q: A badly maintained stair railing breaks and a visitor falls. Who is liable under the Code of Obligations?
130077.e: Owner's liability for structures is strict liability: the owner is liable for damage caused by faulty construction or poor maintenance, even without fault.
130077.m: The owner is liable for defective buildings.

130078.q: Within what period from knowing about the damage and the person responsible does a compensation claim for a wrongful act generally become time-barred?
130078.e: Since 2020 the relative limitation period is three years from knowledge. There is also an absolute period of ten years from the harmful event, twenty years for personal injury.

130079.q: How do basic and supplementary insurance fundamentally differ when accepting people?
a: Only supplementary insurance may take health and risk into account
Only basic insurance may ask health questions
Both must accept everyone without questions
130079.e: Basic insurance must accept everyone without a health check. Supplementary insurance is governed by private law and may ask questions, impose exclusions or refuse.
130079.m: Supplementary may check, basic must accept.

130080.q: Why do health insurance premiums rise in the long term?
a: Because health costs rise, through ageing and medical progress for example
Because insurers must build new offices every year
Because the premium is linked to the petrol price
130080.e: Premiums must cover the costs of basic insurance. More older people, new therapies and more treatments increase these costs.
130080.m: Rising costs lead to rising premiums.

130081.q: Why are there premium reductions, even though everyone pays the same per-person premium?
a: Because the same premium weighs more heavily on people with low incomes
Because rich people pay no premium
Because otherwise insurers make a profit
Because the Confederation pays all premiums
130081.e: The per-person premium does not depend on income. For households with little money it is a large part of the budget, so the Confederation and cantons help.
130081.m: Premium reductions balance the per-person premium socially.

130082.q: Some personal liability policies offer a “waiver of the gross negligence defence”. What does that mean?
a: The insurer does not reduce payment even for gross negligence, usually except with alcohol or drugs
The insurer only pays for deliberate damage
You may never report damage again
130082.e: Without this add-on the insurer may reduce payment for gross negligence. With the waiver it pays in full; exceptions such as alcohol or drugs are in the terms.
130082.m: The waiver protects against cuts for gross negligence.

130083.q: Three students live in a shared flat. What should they consider about household contents insurance?
a: Clarify whether each person insures their own things or a joint solution fits
Only one person may have contents
Health insurance covers shared flat furniture
130083.e: In a shared flat the things belong to different people. Depending on the insurer, each needs their own policy, or there are special shared flat solutions.
130083.m: In a shared flat, sort out insurance deliberately.

130084.q: What does the duty to mitigate damage require of insured people?
a: To do what is reasonable so the damage does not get worse
To report as many claims as possible
To double the premium with each claim
To repair the damage themselves without reporting it
130084.e: After damage you must do what is reasonable, such as turning off the water or drying wet things. Anyone who fails to do this risks a reduction.
130084.m: After damage, do what is reasonable to limit it.

130085.q: What can happen if you report damage to the insurer months later without good reason?
a: The insurer can reduce payment if the delay disadvantages it
130085.e: Damage must be reported quickly. If the delay meant the insurer could no longer properly assess the damage, it may reduce the payment.

130086.q: Why do you choose a high sum insured of several million francs for personal liability insurance?
a: Because personal injuries with lifelong consequences can be very expensive
Because the premium is then lower
Because you get the money back
Because the law forbids exactly 1 million
130086.e: If someone is seriously injured and can no longer work, there are costs for treatment, lost earnings and care. Such damage can run into millions.

130087.q: What happens to surpluses a health insurer makes in basic insurance?
a: They stay in basic insurance, as reserves for example
They are paid out to shareholders
They go into the insurer's advertising
130087.e: Basic insurance is a non-profit social insurance. Surpluses benefit the insured, as reserves or for lower premiums, for example.
130087.m: Basic insurance money stays with the insured.

130088.q: Kim moves out of home at 20 and takes out her own insurance. Which order makes sense?
a: First basic health and personal liability, then contents, then check optional ones
First travel insurance, basic insurance later
None at all as long as Kim is healthy
130088.e: Basic insurance is compulsory, and liability insurance protects against very high claims. Contents and other insurance follow as needed.
130088.m: Insure the most important first, then the optional.

130089.q: Does liability insurance pay a fine you receive from the police for a traffic offence?
a: No, fines are penalties and cannot be insured
Yes, if you pay the excess
130089.e: Insurance replaces damage. A fine is a penalty for your own behaviour and must be paid personally.

130090.q: What does it mean if a hospital is on a canton's hospital list?
a: Basic insurance and the canton pay for inpatient treatment there
The hospital is the largest in the canton
The hospital only accepts private patients
The hospital is only open for emergencies
130090.e: With the hospital list, cantons decide which hospitals may bill basic insurance. There the canton and insurer share the inpatient costs.
130090.m: Listed hospitals bill basic insurance and the canton.

130091.q: Laura is treated in hospital in Thailand after an accident. What helps her most to sort out the costs?
a: Quickly calling the emergency number of her health or travel insurer
Throwing the bills away and reporting it at home
Only asking the embassy for money
130091.e: Insurers' emergency centres give cost guarantees and organise transport home if needed. You should keep the receipts.
130091.m: Abroad, call the insurer's emergency number early.

130092.q: Why should self-employed people consider daily sickness allowance insurance?
a: Because otherwise nobody covers their lost income when ill
Because otherwise they may not have basic insurance
Because the Confederation demands it every year
Because otherwise they may not issue invoices
130092.e: Employees often have continued pay or a daily allowance through the employer. The self-employed bear the risk of lost income themselves.
130092.m: The self-employed insure their lost income themselves.

130093.q: A bill shows a service Simon does not understand. Who must explain the bill to him on request?
a: The provider, such as the doctor's surgery
130093.e: Patients have the right to understand what they are paying for. The surgery or hospital explains the items, and the insurer also helps.

130094.q: Lea hung a few pictures in her rented flat. What usually applies to a few small rawlplug holes when she moves out?
a: They usually count as normal wear and tear from ordinary use
They are always a major liability claim
They must be paid by buildings insurance
They automatically mean losing the whole deposit
130094.e: Hanging pictures is part of normal living. A few small holes to the usual extent are generally not damage, but very many or large holes can be.

130095.q: What is important when moving out of a rented flat so there is no later dispute about damage?
a: Drawing up a handover report together with the landlady
Just putting the key in the letterbox
Leaving the flat without an appointment
130095.e: Defects are recorded and signed in the handover report. If you disagree, you note that before signing.
130095.m: Make a handover report when moving out.

130096.q: Why is a detailed move-in report worthwhile when moving into a rented flat?
a: Because it proves which defects were already there
Because the rent then goes down
Because otherwise you get no electricity
Because the health insurer demands it
130096.e: Defects recorded on moving in do not have to be paid for on moving out. Dated photos help too.

130097.q: Since when have most people in Switzerland had compulsory basic insurance under today's Health Insurance Act (KVG)?
130097.e: The Health Insurance Act came into force in 1996 and made basic insurance compulsory for everyone. Before that it was optional in most cantons.

130098.q: Daniel has had the same sum insured for his contents for ten years but has bought much more since. What is the risk?
a: Underinsurance with reduced payment in a claim
Automatic cancellation of his health insurance
130098.e: If the value of the contents grows but the sum insured does not, you are underinsured. Some insurers waive a reduction for small differences, but you should not rely on it.

130099.q: An adult with a 300 deductible (Franchise) spends 10 days in hospital. The costs are 20,000 francs, and he had no others. How much does he pay himself in total?
130099.e: He pays the deductible of 300 francs and the maximum co-payment of 700 francs. On top come 10 days of hospital contribution at 15 francs, so 150 francs.
130099.m: Add up deductible, co-payment and hospital contribution.

130100.q: A child has a deductible (Franchise) of 600 francs and costs of 10,000 francs in the year. What is the most the parents pay?
130100.e: First the deductible of 600 francs. The co-payment would be 940 francs, but for children it is capped at 350 francs. Together that is 950 francs.
130100.m: For children the co-payment is capped at 350 francs.

130101.q: On holiday Lena's laptop is stolen from her locked hotel room after a break-in. What usually applies?
a: Contents insurance pays, because contents are also insured temporarily away from home
Nobody pays, holidays are never insured
The hotel must always pay for everything
130101.e: With most insurers, contents are also insured while temporarily outside the home, often worldwide. The details are in the terms.
130101.m: Contents are insured temporarily away from home too.

130102.q: Lars moves out of his parents' flat at 22. What should he check about personal liability insurance?
a: Whether he is still covered by the family policy or needs his own
Nothing, liability applies automatically for life through the parents
Whether his health insurer covers liability
Whether the municipality gives him liability cover
130102.e: Family policies usually cover people in the same household. Anyone who moves out is often no longer covered, or only for a short time.
130102.m: Sort out your own liability insurance when moving out.

130103.q: What do the four Swiss German words “warte, luege, lose, laufe” mean?
130103.e: This is how to cross the road safely: first wait at the kerb, look left and right, listen for cars and only then go.

130104.q: A car is coming to the zebra crossing. Why do you look at the driver?
a: To be sure he has seen you
Because it is polite to count cars
130104.e: Only when the car has stopped and the driver has seen you is it safe to go.
130104.m: Only go when the car has stopped.

130105.q: A car is reversing out of a driveway. What do you do?
130105.e: Someone reversing often cannot see children behind the car. So you wait until the car has gone.
130105.m: Behind a reversing car it is dangerous.

130106.q: You get off the bus and want to cross the road. What is right?
a: Wait until the bus has driven off
Run across the road right in front of the bus
Wave to the bus driver and run off
130106.e: The bus hides you, and the cars cannot see you. When the bus has gone, you can see the road well.
130106.m: Only cross once the bus has gone.

130107.q: You want to get off the bus at the next stop. What do you do?
a: Nothing, the bus always stops everywhere
130107.e: With the stop button the driver can see that someone wants to get off.
130107.m: Pressing the stop button means: I want to get off.

130108.q: You are standing on the tram. Why do you hold on to a pole?
a: So you do not fall over when it brakes
Because otherwise the tram will not move
So you can get off faster
130108.e: The tram can brake suddenly. If you hold on, you will not fall over.
130108.m: Always hold on in buses and trams.

130109.q: On the train an elderly woman is standing and cannot find a seat. What is polite?
a: Put your bag on the free seat
130109.e: Older people, people on crutches or with small children often need a seat more.
130109.m: I offer my seat when someone needs it more.

130110.q: Where do you wait for the train at the station?
a: Behind the safety line on the platform
Right at the edge of the platform
130110.e: A train coming in makes a strong wind. Behind the line you are safe.
130110.m: Wait behind the line on the platform.

130111.q: At the level crossing a red light is flashing. What do you do?
a: Walk on if no train can be seen
130111.e: A flashing red light means a train is coming soon. A train cannot brake quickly.
130111.m: Flashing red at a level crossing: stop.

130112.q: Where is it safest to cross the road?
a: At a zebra crossing or traffic lights
130112.e: At zebra crossings and traffic lights, drivers expect pedestrians.
130112.m: I cross the road at the zebra crossing.

130113.q: Why do you not cross the road on a bend?
a: Because you see the cars too late
Because there are too many trees there
Because the ground is slippery there
130113.e: On a bend you cannot see far, and the cars also see you late.
130113.m: You cannot see well on a bend.

130114.q: A big lorry wants to turn. Why do you not stand right next to it?
a: The driver cannot see you there
You are not allowed to look at lorries
130114.e: Beside and in front of a lorry there are places the driver cannot see. This is called the blind spot.
130114.m: Keep your distance from big lorries.

130115.q: The pedestrian light turns green. What do you do?
a: Quickly check that all cars have stopped, then go
Run off with your eyes closed
Wait until it is red again
130115.e: Green means you may go. Even so, you check that all the cars really are stopping.
130115.m: Take a quick look even when it is green.

130116.q: Why do you not ride your bike with headphones on?
a: Because you cannot hear cars and bells
130116.e: In traffic you need to hear what is happening around you, a car coming from behind for example.
130116.m: In traffic, keep your ears free.

130117.q: Why do you check the brakes before riding your bike?
a: So the tyres have more air
130117.e: If the brakes do not work well, you cannot stop in time.

130118.q: Where is the best place to play with your ball?
a: At the playground or in the garden
In the car park between cars
On the pavement next to the station
130118.e: Cars drive on roads and in car parks. At the playground you are safe.
130118.m: Play at the playground, not on the road.

130119.e: Eggshells are natural and break down into soil in the compost.
130119.m: Plant food scraps and eggshells go in the compost.

130120.q: Where do you take an empty aluminium drinks can?
130120.e: Collected aluminium is made into new aluminium. That is why it has its own collection.

130121.q: Your jumper is too small for you, but still nice. What can you do with it?
a: Give it to the clothes collection
Take it to the glass collection
130121.e: Someone else can wear good clothes. That is why there are clothes collections.
130121.m: Pass good clothes on instead of throwing them away.

130122.q: How do you get old newspapers ready for the paper collection?
a: Tied into a bundle with string
Crumpled up in the rubbish bag
130122.e: In many municipalities waste paper is bundled, tied with string and put out by the road.
130122.m: Bundle waste paper and tie it up.

130123.q: Lara simply throws her ice cream wrapper onto the grass. What is this called?
130123.e: Anyone who leaves rubbish lying outside or throws it away is littering. It pollutes nature.
130123.m: Rubbish goes in the bin, not on the ground.

130124.q: Where does an empty tin can go?
130124.e: Tins are made of metal. Once collected, the metal can be used again.
130124.m: Tins go in the scrap metal.

130125.q: When do you put the rubbish bag out in front of the house?
a: On the day of the rubbish collection
Never, you burn it in the garden
130125.e: The municipality collects the rubbish on certain days. Otherwise it lies outside too long and animals tear it open.
130125.m: Only put rubbish out on collection day.

130126.q: What do you stick on a letter before you send it?
130126.e: With the stamp you pay the post for delivering the letter.

130127.q: Where do you stick the stamp on a letter?
a: In the middle of the back
130127.e: The stamp goes on the front, top right. That is where the post looks for it.

130128.q: Bern has the postcode 3000. Where do you write it on the letter?
a: Before the name of the town
On the back on its own
130128.e: In Switzerland the postcode comes directly before the town, for example “3000 Bern”.

130129.q: You want to send a letter with a stamp. Where do you put it?
a: In a yellow Swiss Post postbox
130129.e: Swiss Post postboxes are yellow. The post collects the letters from there.
130129.m: Letters go in the yellow Swiss Post postbox.

130130.q: What belongs in an address on a letter?
a: Name, street with number, postcode and town
130130.e: With the name, street, house number, postcode and town the post finds the right letterbox.
130130.m: An address has name, street, postcode and town.

130131.q: Why is your family name on your letterbox?
a: So the post knows where the letters belong
So the neighbours know your birthday
130131.e: The postman or postwoman looks for the name on the letterbox. If it is missing, a letter may be sent back.
130131.m: Without a name on the letterbox, post struggles to arrive.

130132.q: After you pay, the cashier gives you a small slip of paper. What is on it?
130132.e: That is the receipt. It shows the goods, the price and the date of the purchase.
130132.m: The receipt shows what I paid for.

130133.q: Why do you keep the receipt for new shoes for a while?
a: So you can take them back if there is a problem
So you can show it at school
130133.e: If something breaks or does not fit, the shop usually wants to see the receipt.
130133.m: Keep the receipt in case something is wrong.

130134.q: A loaf of bread costs 3 francs. You pay with a 5-franc coin. How much change do you get?
130134.e: 5 francs minus 3 francs is 2 francs change.
130134.m: Change is what is left after paying.

130135.q: An apple costs 1 franc. How much do 4 apples cost?

130136.q: Why do you take your own bag when shopping?
a: So fewer plastic bags are needed
Because otherwise you may not buy anything
130136.e: A bag can be used many times. That means less rubbish.

130137.q: Why do you write a shopping list before going shopping?
a: So you forget nothing and buy nothing unnecessary
So you can draw in the shop
So you stay longer in the shop
130137.e: The list shows what you really need. That saves time and money.
130137.m: With a shopping list I buy what I need.

130138.q: The shop assistant gives you your change. What do you say?
130138.e: By saying “thank you” you show that you are friendly.

130139.q: You are leaving the bakery. What do you say as you go?
130139.e: You say “Grüezi” (hello) when you arrive; when you leave you say “Uf Wiederluege” or “Adieu”, which means goodbye.
130139.m: When I leave, I say goodbye.

130140.q: You accidentally bump into someone in the corridor. What do you say?
130140.e: If you accidentally disturb or bump into someone, you apologise.
130140.m: Bumped into someone by accident: say sorry.

130141.q: You need to cough. Where do you cough?
a: Into the crook of your elbow
Into your hand and then shake someone's hand
130141.e: Coughing into the crook of your elbow spreads fewer germs onto hands and objects.
130141.m: Cough and sneeze into the crook of your elbow.

130142.q: The door to your sister's room is shut. What do you do before going in?
130142.e: Knocking shows respect. The other person can say “come in”.

130143.q: You answer the phone at home. How do you answer politely?
130143.e: Then the caller knows straight away who they are talking to.
130143.m: On the phone I say my name.

130144.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland to call the police?
130144.e: 117 is the police emergency number. 118 is the fire brigade, 144 the ambulance.

130145.q: You have called the emergency number and told them everything. When do you hang up?
a: Only when the person on the phone says so
When you no longer feel like it
130145.e: The emergency centre often has more questions. So you wait until they end the call.
130145.m: On an emergency call I do not hang up first.

130146.q: Why should you know your address by heart?
a: So you can say where you live in an emergency
So you can send it to strangers online
Because you need it in PE
So you can write it on walls
130146.e: If you call for help or get lost, you need to be able to say where you live.
130146.m: I know my address by heart.

130147.q: Why is it good to know your parents' mobile number by heart?
a: So you can call them even without your own phone
So you can share it in a chat
So you can use it as a password in games
Because otherwise their phone does not ring
130147.e: If your phone is flat or lost, you can call your parents from another phone.
130147.m: I know my parents' number by heart.

130148.q: On the way to school you find a purse. What do you do?
a: Hand it in to the police or the lost property office
Throw it in the nearest bin
130148.e: What you find belongs to someone else. At the lost property office or the police the person can collect it.
130148.m: I hand in what I find.

130149.q: You smell smoke and see fire in the flat. What do you do first?
a: Get out quickly and warn adults
130149.e: Smoke is very dangerous. First you get yourself to safety and call for help.
130149.m: In a fire, get out first.

130150.q: In a game someone you do not know wants to add you as a friend. What do you do?
a: Send them your name and school
Send them a photo of yourself
130150.e: Online you never know for sure who someone really is. Only accept people you know.
130150.m: Online I only accept people I know.

130151.q: A message pops up on the tablet: “You have won a phone! Click here!” What do you do?
a: Do not click and ask an adult
Send the link to all your friends
130151.e: Messages like this are almost always a trick to get data or money.
130151.m: Too good to be true: do not click.

130152.q: Why do you put the tablet away before going to sleep?
a: So you can fall asleep more easily
So you are more tired in the morning
130152.e: Bright screens and exciting games keep you awake. Without a screen you sleep more peacefully.

130153.q: School starts at 8 o'clock. Your walk to school takes 15 minutes. What is the latest time you must leave?
130153.e: 8 o'clock minus 15 minutes is 7.45. A little earlier is even better.
130153.m: I allow time for the journey so I am on time.

130154.q: In German, people say “halb acht”. What time is that?
130154.e: “Halb acht” means half an hour before eight o'clock, so 7.30. In British English you might also hear “half seven”.

130155.q: Today is Monday. On Wednesday you have swimming. In how many days is that?
130155.e: After Monday comes Tuesday, then Wednesday. That is 2 days.

130156.q: You have a dentist's appointment tomorrow but you are ill. What do you do?
a: Cancel the appointment by phone in good time
130156.e: If you cancel early, someone else can have the appointment. That is polite.
130156.m: Cannot make an appointment: cancel early.

130157.q: Why does a family calendar hang in the kitchen?
a: So everyone can see who has an appointment when
So you can cook on it
So you can give it to the neighbours
130157.e: The calendar shows birthdays, training or doctor's appointments. That way nobody forgets anything.

130158.q: Your building has a laundry rota for the shared laundry room. What is it for?
a: It shows who may do their washing when
It shows which clothes are nice
It says when the post comes
130158.e: In many blocks of flats everyone shares one laundry room. The rota sets out whose turn it is.
130158.m: The rota shares the laundry room fairly.

130159.q: You are leaving your room for a long time. What do you do with the light?
130159.e: Light that nobody needs uses electricity for nothing.
130159.m: Lights off when I go out.

130160.q: How do you save water when brushing your teeth?
a: Turn off the tap while you brush
Leave the water running the whole time
130160.e: While you brush you do not need running water. You only turn it on again to rinse.

130161.q: Why do you not run and shout in the stairwell?
a: Because it is noisy for everyone in the building
Because stairs are only for adults
130161.e: In the stairwell every noise can be heard in many flats. Keeping quiet is considerate.
130161.m: I am quiet in the stairwell.

130162.q: Your neighbour is carrying heavy shopping bags up the stairs. What can you do?
a: Shut the door in front of her
130162.e: Neighbours are glad to help each other. Asking is friendly.

130163.q: The doorbell rings and you are home alone. What do you do?
a: Do not open the door and call your parents
Shout out of the window that you are alone
130163.e: When you are alone, you do not open the door to strangers. Your parents will tell you what to do.
130163.m: Home alone: do not open to strangers.

130164.q: Why do you not hang your house key visibly on the outside of your school bag?
a: So strangers cannot see it and take it
Because the school bag cannot take it
130164.e: You keep the key well hidden in your bag so nobody can steal it.

130165.q: The post brings a parcel. How does it know whom it is for?
a: From the address on the parcel
From the colour of the parcel
From the weight of the parcel
From the size of the box
130165.e: Every parcel has the address of the person it is for.
130165.m: The address says where the parcel goes.

130166.q: What is the sender on a letter?
a: The person who sends the letter
The person who receives the letter
130166.e: The sender sends the letter. If it is written on it, the letter can come back if it does not arrive.

130167.q: You are on holiday and want to write to your grandmother. What can you send?
130167.e: You write a short greeting on a postcard, stick on a stamp and post it.
130167.m: Holiday greetings go on a postcard.

130168.q: Where can you buy a ticket at the station?
130168.e: Stations have ticket machines. Many people also buy their ticket with an app.
130168.m: Buy your ticket before the journey, at the machine or in the app.

130169.q: On the train you see the sign “Quiet zone”. What does it mean?
a: Here you are quiet and do not make phone calls
Here you may listen to loud music
Here you may sleep and snore
130169.e: In the quiet zone people want to read, work or rest.

130170.q: Why do you not put your shoes on the seat opposite on the train?
a: Because the seat gets dirty for the next person
Because otherwise your shoes get cold
Because you must be barefoot on the train
130170.e: Someone else wants to sit on the seat afterwards without getting dirt on their clothes.

130171.q: You have lost your family at the station. Whom do you ask for help?
a: A stranger who wants to take you with him
130171.e: Railway staff wear a uniform and can have your family called over the loudspeaker.

130172.q: You leave your bike outside school. What do you do?
a: Leave it in the middle of the path
130172.e: With a lock your bike is not so easily stolen.

130173.q: It is getting dark and you are still riding your bike. What do you switch on?
130173.e: With lights the others can see you and you can see the way.
130173.m: In the dark, bike lights on.

130174.q: Your friend wants a ride on your bike's luggage rack. What do you say?
a: No, that is dangerous and not allowed
Yes, if he holds on tight
130174.e: There is only room for one person on a normal bike. Passengers on the luggage rack can fall off.
130174.m: Only I ride on my bike.

130175.q: You are riding your scooter on the pavement. What do you pay attention to?
a: To pedestrians, and you go slowly
To going as fast as possible
To riding in the middle of the road
130175.e: Pedestrians walk on the pavement. On your scooter you are considerate.

130176.q: When do you fasten your seat belt in the car?
a: Before setting off, on every journey
130176.e: Something can happen even on short trips. So the rule is: always buckle up.

130177.q: Which side do you get out of the car when it is parked at the roadside?
130177.e: Cars and bikes drive past on the road side. On the pavement side you are safe.
130177.m: Get out on the pavement side.

130178.q: May a plastic bag go in with the green waste?
a: No, plastic does not break down
130178.e: Green waste is turned into compost or gas. Plastic does not break down and pollutes the soil.
130178.m: No plastic in the green waste.

130179.q: What do you do with a big cardboard box before it goes to the cardboard collection?
a: Tear it into small pieces and set fire to it
130179.e: Cardboard folded flat takes up much less space.

130180.q: Why do you not put glass, paper and PET all in the same bag?
a: So the material can be used again
130180.e: Glass, paper, aluminium and PET can be recycled if they are collected separately. Then fewer new raw materials are needed.

130181.q: An empty jam jar is still whole. What can you do before throwing it away?
a: Use it again, for pens for example
Put it in the green waste
130181.e: If something can be used again, you do not need to throw it away. That saves rubbish.
130181.m: Reuse first, then dispose of it properly.

130182.q: What does the date on a yoghurt pot show?
a: Until when the yoghurt is definitely good
130182.e: Food packaging shows how long the food keeps.
130182.m: The date on food shows how long it keeps.

130183.q: What do you put on the belt at the checkout?
a: The things you want to buy
130183.e: At the checkout the cashier scans the goods and tells you the price.
130183.m: At the checkout I put the goods on the belt.

130184.q: Three people are already waiting at the till. What do you do?
a: Join the back of the queue
Push in right at the front
Pass your goods over people's heads
130184.e: First come, first served. You join the back of the queue.
130184.m: I join the back of the queue.

130185.q: One exercise book costs 2 francs, another 5 francs. How much do you save with the cheaper one?
130185.e: 5 francs minus 2 francs is a difference of 3 francs.

130186.q: You want a game that costs 20 francs. You get 5 francs every week. After how many weeks do you have enough?
130186.m: Saving helps me reach my goal.

130187.q: You would like someone to pass you the bread. How do you ask?
a: “Could you pass me the bread, please?”
You reach across the others' plates
130187.e: With “please” you ask in a friendly way.

130188.q: At the table you still have food in your mouth. What is polite?
a: Talk loudly with your mouth full
130188.e: Talking with your mouth full is unpleasant for the others.

130189.q: Someone is telling you something. How do you show you are listening?
a: You look at the person and do not interrupt
You talk at the same time
130189.e: A good listener looks at the other person and lets them finish.
130189.m: Listening well means letting people finish.

130190.q: You are invited to a birthday party but cannot come. What do you do?
a: Let them know beforehand that you are not coming
130190.e: The host wants to be able to plan. So you let them know in good time.

130191.q: Your friend takes a funny photo of you and wants to post it in the class chat. What may you say?
a: That you do not want that
That he should send it to all strangers
That he should add your password
130191.e: Others may not simply share photos of you if you do not want them to.
130191.m: I have a say about photos of me.

130192.q: How do you write in the class chat?
a: In a friendly way, just as you talk in real life
With insults, that is allowed in chats
Only in capital letters, because it is louder
Lots of messages in the middle of the night
130192.e: Behind every message there is a person. Mean words hurt in a chat too.
130192.m: In chats I am as nice as in real life.

130193.q: A stranger sends you a link. What do you do?
a: Do not open it and show your parents
Forward it to everyone in the class
130193.e: Links from strangers can be dangerous or lead to bad websites.
130193.m: I do not open links from strangers.

130194.q: Which name is best for an online game?
a: Your full first name and surname
130194.e: A made-up name does not give away who you are or where you live.
130194.m: Online I use a made-up name.

130195.q: You have played enough and it is time to eat. What do you do?
a: End the game and come to the table
Keep playing and forget the meal
Bring the tablet to the table
130195.e: At family meals the screen is off so everyone can talk to each other.
130195.m: At meals the screen is off.

130196.q: What must you definitely say on an emergency call?
130196.e: The rescuers need to know where to go. That is why the place is very important.
130196.m: On an emergency call I say where I am.

130197.q: A child has fallen off the climbing frame and is crying a lot. What do you do first?
130197.e: An adult can check whether the child is hurt and call for help.
130197.m: In an accident I fetch an adult.

130198.q: Why do you never put anything metal into a socket?
a: Because you can get a dangerous electric shock
Because otherwise the socket gets dirty
Because the light then turns colourful
Because the socket then gets cold
130198.e: Electricity flows in the socket. Metal conducts electricity straight into your body.
130198.m: Never put anything into a socket.

130199.q: An adult you do not know offers you sweets and wants you to come with him. What do you do?
a: Say no, walk away and tell someone at home
Go with him because he is nice
Take the sweets and go with him
130199.e: You never go with strangers. Tell your parents or your teacher straight away.

130200.q: Why do kindergarten children often wear a bright triangle or vest on their way?
a: So drivers can see them well
Because it is a uniform for parties
130200.e: Bright colours catch drivers' eyes early, even in fog or rain.

130201.q: Why is it good to walk to school?
a: You get exercise and learn about traffic
Because the school always demands it
130201.e: On foot you get exercise, meet friends and learn how to behave in traffic.
130201.m: Walking to school does you good.

130202.q: After washing your hands the water is still running. What do you do?
a: Leave it running for the next person
130202.e: Running water that nobody needs is wasteful.

130203.q: Up to which birthday do children travel at the child fare on Swiss public transport?
130203.e: Children from 6 years old pay the child fare on public transport until they turn 16. After that the adult fare applies.

130204.q: On which card are travelcards such as the Half Fare or GA stored in Switzerland?
130204.e: The SwissPass is the card for public transport travelcards. It is scanned during ticket checks.
130204.m: Public transport travelcards are on the SwissPass.

130205.q: What is typical of a rail saver ticket (Sparbillett)?
a: It is cheaper but only valid on a particular train
It is valid for a whole year
You can travel as often as you like with it
130205.e: Saver tickets are discounted, but you are tied to the connection you chose.
130205.m: Saver ticket: cheaper, but tied to the train.

130206.q: What does a fare network bring to a region?
a: One ticket is valid for bus, tram and train together
You may only travel by bike
Every means of transport needs its own ticket
Public transport is free on Sundays
130206.e: In a fare network the transport companies work together. You buy one ticket for the zones and may change.
130206.m: In a fare network one ticket covers all transport.

130207.q: On the platform there are big letters such as A, B, C, D. What are these sectors for?
a: They show where each carriage stops
130207.e: The display shows in which sector first class or the dining car stops, for example.
130207.m: The sector shows where my carriage stops.

130208.q: What does “connection” mean in the timetable?
a: A train or bus you can change onto directly
The last station on a line
130208.e: A connection is the service that continues after you change.
130208.m: Connection: here I change and travel on.

130209.q: What can you do with a day pass on public transport?
a: Travel as much as you like within its area for one day
130209.e: A day pass is valid for a whole day. You can get on and off as often as you like.
130209.m: Day pass: travel for one day.

130210.q: Elias wants to take his ordinary bike on the train. What does he usually need?
a: A separate ticket for the bike
130210.e: For an ordinary bike you normally need a bike ticket or a bike day pass on the train.
130210.m: A bike on the train usually needs its own ticket.

130211.q: Until when do children in Switzerland need a child seat in the car?
a: Until 12 years old or 150 cm tall
130211.e: Children under 12 who are shorter than 150 cm must travel in a suitable child seat.
130211.m: Child seat until 12 years or 150 cm.

130212.q: What is the speed limit for cars in an encounter zone (Begegnungszone)?
130212.e: In an encounter zone the limit is 20 km/h. Pedestrians have priority there.

130213.q: In a 30 km/h zone there are usually no zebra crossings. What applies to pedestrians?
a: They may cross anywhere but do not have priority
They may not cross the road at all
130213.e: In 30 km/h zones you may cross the road anywhere, but you must let vehicles pass.
130213.m: 30 zone: cross anywhere, but without priority.

130214.q: Where do you ride your bike on the road?
a: As far right as possible, a little away from the edge
In the middle of the lane
130214.e: Bikes ride on the right. A little distance from the edge protects you from drain covers and car doors.

130215.q: Why do you not ride very close past parked cars?
a: Because a car door could suddenly open
Because otherwise the cars get scratched
Because otherwise the alarm goes off
130215.e: An opening car door is a common cause of accidents. With some distance you have time to react.
130215.m: Keep your distance from parked cars.

130216.q: At the station your train shows “+5'”. What does that mean?
a: The train is about 5 minutes late
130216.e: With “+5'” the display shows a delay of about 5 minutes.

130217.q: The post tried to deliver a parcel but nobody was home. What do you find in the letterbox?
130217.e: With the collection notice you can pick up the parcel at the post office or a collection point.
130217.m: Nobody home: collection notice in the letterbox.

130218.q: What is a parcel's tracking number for?
a: You can follow where the parcel is right now
It is the price of the parcel
It is the post office's phone number
